Independent Representation, Not Agendas

Proactive Communication & Year-Round Commitment

My mandate is simple: bring people together rather than campaign on hot-button topics. Proactive transparency on City plans, projects, and bylaws isn't an extra service, it is an elected official's core job.

As your City Councillor, my commitment lasts all four years:

• No Surprises: Clear, upfront communication on local projects before shovels hit the ground.

sources.text:
North Vancouver deserves a City Council that listens before decisions are made — not after. Sean Alexander is running to bring residents back into the process and make sure every voice is heard.

Watch Sean discuss his campaign and his vision for a stronger, more connected North Vancouver.

Residents should hear about major decisions before they feel like a done deal.

The number one concern Sean hears from residents is that City Hall can feel distant from everyday people. Too often, residents find out about decisions affecting traffic, housing, planning, infrastructure, and neighbourhood life only after the process feels complete.

Sean’s campaign is built around a simple promise: listen first, communicate early, and bring community voices directly into City Hall.

Sean’s platform is a living framework shaped by public engagement, door knocking, community meetings, and everyday conversations with residents.

Sean’s path to public service began with a belief that leadership starts with listening and rolling up your sleeves. He has been involved in democratic and grassroots work since 2006, from door knocking and phone calling to campaign organizing and community mobilization.

Sean moved to North Vancouver in 2011 and found a place that felt like home. Since then, he has built his life around community service, professional trust, and showing up for neighbours.

A living platform built through conversations with residents.

Sean is not running to impose a rigid platform from behind closed doors. He is running to create a safer forum for facts, discussion, and practical solutions.

Citizens should know what is happening before decisions are made — not after. Sean will prioritize clear communication, early engagement, and accountable decision-making.

Traffic and traffic calming belong in one practical conversation: congestion, safer streets, transit connections, active transportation, and neighbourhood mobility.

Everyone deserves to feel safe in neighbourhoods, parks, public spaces, and business districts, with prevention-focused and community-minded solutions.

Residents deserve transparency and confidence that public dollars are spent wisely, fairly, and with clear accountability for infrastructure costs.

Protect what makes North Vancouver one of Canada’s best places to live while ensuring seniors, families, renters, homeowners, and future generations can thrive.

The best solutions come from bringing people together and listening to those most affected before policy choices are finalized.

background.quote: I’ve worked to support responsible growth that protects what we value about our community, while ensuring we don’t place unnecessary burdens on residents.
I’m running for another term on City Council because our city is at a critical point.
I’m committed to continuing this work with steady, thoughtful leadership and bringing my experience in business, education and community leadership to the role.

I began my career as a hairstylist, then moved into education, teaching at Carson Graham Secondary School. In 1998, I left teaching to pursue a master’s degree in education, which ultimately led me to open Holly’s Salon and School on central Lonsdale. I owned and operated the business for 20 years, building it into a successful salon and training facility. Along the way, I was recognized by Chatelaine as one of Canada’s most inspirational women. I was also honoured to receive the North Vancouver Chamber of Commerce Business Excellence Awards for “Best Employer” and “Business Person of the Year,” and to be named twice as a finalist for the YWCA Women of Distinction Awards.

Over the years, I’ve been proud to support many local organizations dedicated to strengthening our community and improving the lives of residents, including Community Cares, North Shore Neighbourhood House, the ALS Society, Abreast in a Boat, Cops for Cancer, Jewels for a Cause, and initiatives supporting women in the Downtown East Side.
I was born and raised in North Vancouver, and I’ve built both my career and my family life here on the North Shore.

positions.quote: We’re experiencing continued growth, and with it come real challenges—from keeping our neighbourhoods safe and managing tax dollars responsibly to making smart infrastructure decisions. I’ve worked to support responsible growth that protects what we value about our community, while ensuring we don’t place unnecessary burdens on residents.

Redevelopment of ​Capilano Mall Ensuring the responsible redevelopment of Capilano Mall and surrounding lands is essential. The current plan proposes multiple residential towers, with a mix of condominiums, rental housing, and workforce housing, along with retail space, a community centre, and a public park. Now in the planning and public consultation phase, this project is expected to be one of the largest single redevelopments in our city. It is important that we work with the developer to ensure it is supported by the necessary infrastructure and amenities, and that it reflects the long-term interests of our community.

I believe in accountability, transparency and making decisions that serve the long-term interests of our community—not just short-term fixes.

My experience allows me to ask the right questions, advocate for responsible solutions and stay focused on what matters most to residents.

Build on our relationships and partnerships with community members ​ During the last term, City Council held regular meetings with School District 44, Squamish Nation, and Tsleil-Waututh Nation. These conversations have been very informative, and it is important that we continue this path. We must also include the District of North Vancouver and the District of West Vancouver. We are the North Shore, and we all succeed when we work together. ​

Keeping the North Shore Moving Anyone who has been stuck in traffic knows how frustrating it can be. When there’s an accident or stalled vehicle on one of our bridges, the impact is felt across the entire community. While we’re making it easier to get around by walking, cycling, and transit, we also need to tackle the bigger transportation challenges that require provincial and federal action. Reducing congestion at the Ironworkers Memorial Bridge must be a priority. Our three North Shore municipalities need to work together with provincial and federal partners to pursue the best long-term solution—whether that means additional lanes, better transit, or a new bridge.

Creating more affordable and diverse housing options We’ve made meaningful progress in expanding rental housing, but there is still more work to do. I will continue to support the creation of more affordable and diverse housing options by advocating for below-market units in new developments, protecting and expanding our rental stock, and encouraging a range of housing choices—including rent-to-own, basement suites, coach houses and coach house stratification, lock-off suites, and workforce housing. I also support pre-zoning areas to allow for smaller lots and more attainable housing options.

Reduce homelessness This is a significant and growing challenge for our community. We need more emergency shelter space on the North Shore, as well as regular access to warming centres—not only during extreme weather. I support expanding services within shelters, including access to meals and programs that help people re-enter the workforce. I will continue working with local and provincial partners to strengthen these supports and build a healthier, more inclusive community.

Supporting seniors Seniors make up a growing and important part of our North Shore community, and they deserve to be recognized and supported. As this population continues to grow, we need to do more to ensure access to affordable housing, appropriate services, and meaningful social programs. I will continue working with all levels of government and local businesses to help provide the supports seniors need to live comfortably and to age in place within our community.

Seniors make up a growing and important part of our North Shore community, and they deserve to be recognized and supported.

​Advocating for youth Youth and young adults face a unique set of challenges and priorities. Issues such as climate change, waste reduction, inclusion, and access to affordable healthcare and mental health supports are top of mind. I look forward to continuing to work alongside younger members of our community to help advance these priorities and ensure their voices are heard. I also want to encourage more young adults to get involved in municipal politics and help shape the future of our community.

The Lonsdale Great Street Project is an opportunity to transform Central Lonsdale into a vibrant neighbourhood hub — a place where people can live, work, shop, dine, and gather, while also creating a welcoming destination for visitors. To support this vision, we also launched the Central Lonsdale Business Improvement Area (BIA) in partnership with local business representatives, helping strengthen and promote the area’s economic vitality. ​
This must also include greater focus on substance use education in our schools, helping to build awareness, prevention, and support for young people.

sources.text:
Proven independent leadership for the City of North Vancouver.

It has been a privilege to serve my community as a member of City Council.

I approach each issue before Council by listening carefully to the public, applying independent thinking, common sense, and using my experience in local government and business to seek the best decisions for our community.

There are many issues that I believe must continue to be priorities for the next Council term: increasing traffic congestion; rat-running vehicles through side streets; better parking solutions and regulations; future plans for Central Lonsdale; safer streets, paths, and sidewalks; mitigating conflicts between cars, pedestrians, cyclists and electric scooters. In addition, the need for truly affordable and workforce housing to help keep people on the North Shore; climate change action; increased child care; protecting mature trees; reducing tax increases for both residents and businesses; and more effective public engagement and transparency on major issues.

I support a truly independent public inquiry about Waste Water Treatment Plant costs, reducing future financial impact on our taxpayers and a review of Metro Vancouver Regional District structure.

I ask for your vote to continue serving you. Please contact me by phone or email to discuss any issues.

While listening to and talking with many residents and businesses, I’ve identified the following as key areas of focus for the coming term of Council:

I support more effective direct public engagement and transparency with better opportunities for residents to connect with Council on major policy issues.

Housing in all forms has become unaffordable for an increasing number of people. I support a range of options that could help keep North Vancouver livable for both existing and future residents.

There are no simple solutions to the complex problems of traffic congestion that affect everyone, but there are opportunities to improve the situation.

Recreation and sports facilities, courts, and community parks must continue to be increased to serve the needs of our growing population.

Pay parking was introduced to tackle legitimate issues, but created unintended consequences which can be mitigated with some adjustments.

I want to improve protection of existing mature trees and expand our City tree canopy, in addition to supporting other policies that preserve our environment.

Don Bell has been a resident of North Vancouver for over 50 years, and has lived for the last twelve years in the Central Lonsdale area. He has extensive business, community and local political experience. Prior to his political career, Don owned and operated a small retail business in North Vancouver and for 13 years was in corporate management at Canada Safeway.

background.quote: She served six years on the Social Planning Advisory Committee, including her final two years as Chair, and serves on the Advisory Planning Commission.
For the past eight years, I've had the privilege of serving our community through City advisory committees, local organizations, volunteer initiatives, and grassroots projects.
As a leadership coach and non-profit founder, Anna advances food security and children’s wellbeing, connecting organizations serving families through the North Shore Kids Festival.

As an international leadership coach, Anna works with executives, entrepreneurs, and professionals across North America, Europe, Asia, and Australia, helping people navigate change, make thoughtful decisions, strengthen leadership, and build resilient organizations.
Anna lives her values through year-round public service: give where you live, support local, and commit to the place you choose to call home.

She also serves on the Board of Directors of the International Coaching Federation British Columbia chapter as Membership Director, supporting one of Canada's largest professional coaching communities.

Throughout her career, Anna has brought together local government, businesses, schools, non-profit organizations, volunteers, and residents to turn ideas into meaningful community impact. background.quote: I grew up on a street where neighbours looked after each other — and after 40 years of asking questions for a living, I'm running for CNV Council to help this city do the same.
For four years I’ve been digging into North Vancouver — its finances, its plans, its future — and putting it in plain language. It’s all here, free. No ticket, no paywall.

positions.quote:
I found a City that can do big things, but often decides the big things before listening to the people who’ll live with them.

I’m running for a way of deciding — define the goal, look at the evidence, be honest about who pays, and account for the result. That’s a Vital North Vancouver: a city where the small things work and the big decisions make sense. Where we’re serious about Safety, Economy and Family — and where Trust, Accountability and Transparency aren’t slogans, but how business gets done.

From cleaner sidewalks to smarter spending, I applythe GUIDE test before making a major decision. The five questions I ask: Is it Grounded ? Is it Understandable ? Is it Inclusive ? Is it Doable ? How will it be Evaluated ? Good decisions should pass every one.

But there is another question that deserves equal attention: What happens to mobility in a city that already struggles with congestion?

E-Bikes, Scooters & Pedestrian Safety: A Growing North Shore Problem. This video examines a growing issue facing cities across Canada: fast-moving e-bikes and scooters sharing unmanaged space with pedestrians. This is not a war on bikes. And it is not an anti-car argument. It is a practical discussion about speed, enforcement, safety, and how cities adapt when technology changes faster than infrastructure and policy.

What you see today on Central Lonsdale may be a preview of its future. City Council has endorsed the Lonsdale Great Street Project — a long-term vision to transform the heart of North Vancouver. But what was actually approved? And does this plan reflect the reality of this city — today?
The City's new Parks & Public Space Plan asks an important question: If we can't create many new parks, can streets do some of the work? More greenery. More gathering spaces. More public life.

As a mom with a young daughter, I’ve lived this. Finding daycare, before-school and after-school care in the City is hard, and the waitlists are long.

A healthy city also needs healthy people. B.C. will begin licensing psychotherapists in November 2027, and the standards deciding who qualifies are being consulted on this fall. MY PRIORITIES Affordable Housing · Child Care • Climate Action · Economic and Cultural Development • Traffic, Mobility, and Transit · Indigenous Reconciliation • Listening to You

The City is the economic centre of the North Shore. What happens on Lonsdale, at the Shipyards and along the waterfront determines whether people can build a career here or must commute out of the community to find one.

We’ve seen what focused investment does. The same approach works elsewhere.

Mid-market rentals — for low-and moderate-income earners who don’t earn enough to afford today’s market rents

Family-friendly rentals (3+ bedrooms) — for renting families who need more space

Senior-oriented housing — for seniors looking to stay in the community as their needs change

Rent-to-own options — for first-time buyers who can’t assemble a down payment

Flexible and multi-generational forms — townhouses, cohousing, duplexes, and homes with secondary suites or coach houses that can serve as a mortgage helper or let family members age in place

Time and again I hear from North Vancouver residents who are leaving our City for more affordable communities. Many of them still work here; they’ve simply traded a home they can afford for a long commute on and off the North Shore. Incomes are not keeping pace with the cost of housing.

Employers see the same problem from the other side. In conversations with local businesses, the North Vancouver Chamber of Commerce, not-for-profits and emergency service providers, I hear a consistent concern: without housing their staff can afford, they struggle to recruit and keep people. That matters most where it’s least visible. When the people who staff our fire halls, care homes and childcare centres can’t afford to live in the community they serve, it isn’t only an employer problem — it’s a community resilience problem. It also puts more cars on the bridges every day.

The pressure on existing tenants is just as real. As land and construction costs rise, much of our remaining affordable rental stock is aging. Those tenants face steady rent increases, the threat of renoviction, and displacement when older buildings are redeveloped. That’s why I brought forward a motion to strengthen the supports and amounts developers must pay to tenants being displaced due to rental redevelopments.

There is no single fix. On Council I’ve supported the housing agreements, zoning changes and provincial alignment work that get the housing we need built. These efforts have had an impact over the past eight years. Our City now offers:

The most affordable rental prices on the North Shore* (but still out of reach for many)

The only North Shore municipality to meet the provincial housing directive for more housing – and we’re exceeding it!

A 450% increase in three-bedroom rental homes for families *

Upcoming cooling strategy for better temperature cooling for multi-unit buildings

If re-elected, I’ll keep pushing to make sure what gets built is what our community actually needs.

Unable to realize alternative accommodation after trying for many years, a younger neighbour friend sent me to Angela for assistance in the difficult situation of our displacement for redevelopment, my second such experience on the North Shore. Angela encouraged me in a situation I had known nothing about, namely that new developers are required to have a few spaces at a lower price for tenants they were displacing. Angela went to bat for me with one of the leasing agents for the developer company. They decided they were able to accept me at a price I could manage. Delivery of the City’s Child Care Action Plan — Council approved this ten-year strategy; the job now is implementation. Read the plan

More child care on City-owned land — expand public spaces operated by non-profit providers

Child care in new developments — secure spaces through the rezoning process, so care exists where families actually live

Stronger partnerships — press senior governments for the capital funding that builds new spaces, and work with local providers to improve quality and access

As a mom with a young daughter, I’ve lived this. Finding daycare, before-school and after-school care in the City is hard, and the waitlists are long. Parents I talk to are driving to other municipalities for a space and it’s adding an hour to their day and disrupting the routines that young children depend on. Providers who want to expand here often can’t, because there’s nowhere suitable to do it. That last problem is one the City can actually solve. Land and space are municipal levers. When we make City-owned sites available to non-profit operators and secure child care space as new housing is approved, we create the conditions providers need to grow and expand.

The timing matters. Provincial and federal capital funding for new spaces is available now, and municipalities that come forward with sites and shovel-ready proposals are the ones that get it. On Council, I moved, along with former Councillor Tina Hu, to explore a co-ordinated after-school program initiative with key partners in the City to find creative ways to create more options for working parents not to have to leave work to get their school aged children into a program from school.

I also moved the additional funding that delivered a 37-space child care facility at Mahon Park. I also advocated for and supported securing $3.5 million in City funding for a 37-space child care centre for ages 0-5 at Cloverley Elementary, and up to 50-space after school care for students at this school. I want to keep this work going – because every year we wait is another cohort of families having to commute elsewhere to meet their childcare needs.

Angela Girard is very close to my heart. During our time serving together on North Vancouver City Council, we laughed together, cried together, and achieved many meaningful things for our community.

Professionally, Angela is hardworking, caring, and deeply committed to the residents she serves. Personally, she is kind, genuine, and compassionate. It is this rare combination of dedication and humanity that makes her exactly the kind of councillor our city needs.

Angela is never afraid to stand up for residents when they raise concerns. She takes the time to listen, understand their experiences, and advocate for the support our city needs from senior levels of government. Whether we were working on childcare initiatives, after-school care, multicultural events, or other community priorities, Angela always brought passion, energy, and a determination to turn ideas into action. I have seen firsthand how much she cares about North Vancouver and the people who call it home. I would not hesitate for a second to support Angela Girard for City Councillor.

Prepare for the heat we’re already getting — expand tree canopy and shade, and make sure cooling spaces are open, staffed and known to residents during extreme heat events

Grow the urban forest — deliver on the City’s 24% canopy target, which cools streets, manages stormwater and cleans the air

Build for wildfire smoke and heavy rain — clean air spaces during smoke season, and stormwater infrastructure sized for the rainfall we now get, not the rainfall we used to get

Hold to our emissions targets — Council set community-wide reduction goals in 2019; the work now is implementation, and reporting honestly on progress

Deliver the Climate and Environment Strategy — the adopted strategy sets the actions; the job is funding and executing them

Prepare for the heat we're already getting — expand tree canopy and shade, and make sure cooling spaces are open, staffed and known to residents during extreme heat events

Grow the urban forest — deliver on the City's 24% canopy target, which cools streets, manages stormwater and cleans the air

The climate isn’t changing somewhere else. It’s changing here: hotter summers, smoke that keeps people indoors for weeks, and rainfall our drainage was never designed to handle. Those aren’t forecasts. They’re the last several summers.

Some of that warming is already locked in, which is why resilience and emissions reduction have to happen together. Cutting carbon is how we do our part to limit how bad it gets. Adapting is how we protect people in the meantime and the people most at risk are the ones least able to buy their way out of it: seniors in older apartments without cooling, people with asthma, outdoor workers.

The good news is that the local work is practical. Trees, shade, cooling and clean air spaces, and drainage that can handle a storm are things a City Council decides on and pays for.

Last term, while a member of the City’s Advisory Design Panel, I advocated for buildings with greater overhangs and larger openable windows, as well as designs which supported the retention of trees where possible. I also supported the City’s first tree protection bylaw to protect our tree canopy on private property, in multi-family residential, commercial, civic, industrial and mixed employment areas across the city. This means that any tree at or greater than 20cm diameter at breast height (1.4 metres) will require a permit for removal, even if there is no active development taking place.

This term, I supported the Urban Forest Directions Report and the City’s new 24% canopy target, backed by stronger tree protection. This new target would add 24,800 new trees to the City’s urban environment.

I also brought forward a motion for a City Cooling Strategy — a maximum indoor temperature of 26°C in existing apartment buildings, and provincial changes so that no landlord or strata can stop a resident from using a portable cooling device.

A person shouldn’t need permission to keep their home survivable in a heat wave.

That’s the direction I want to keep pushing: fewer targets on paper, more protection where people live.

Angela is a strong leader for affordable housing, child care and climate adaptation issues. Her initiatives and voting record highlight integrity and her desire to improve the community in every way.
sources.title: Climate Action - Angela Girard, City of North Vancouver

sources.text:
Cut the barriers small businesses face — faster permitting, clearer requirements, and a City that’s easier to deal with when you’re trying to open or expand

Back our Business Improvement Areas — continue supporting the successful work of the Lower Lonsdale BIA in the Shipyards District, and support the new Central Lonsdale BIA , now up and running, to make sure it thrives

Deliver the Lonsdale Great Street Plan — redefine the City’s central commercial corridor so it draws people in and keeps local businesses busy

Grow the Health Innovation District — build on Lions Gate Hospital and the health businesses and organizations clustered around Central Lonsdale to anchor health-sector jobs, investment and better health outcomes in the City

Expand the Brewery District, and develop marine and technology employment in Lower Lonsdale — distinct districts give businesses a reason to cluster here rather than across the bridge

Build the cultural precinct as a destination — MONOVA, the Polygon Gallery, Presentation House, North Van Arts and the private galleries around them are economic assets for the City as much as cultural ones

Launch a multi-day annual multicultural community festival — showcasing the many cultures in our city through local artists and performers, with local businesses both supporting it and benefiting from it

Keep working with the North Shore Chamber of Commerce and local business — the owners and the people running businesses here know what’s holding them back

Speak up for accessible mental health care — as B.C. finalizes psychotherapy licensing for 2027, press the Province to recognize the full range of therapeutic approaches so residents can find qualified care that fits them

The City is the economic centre of the North Shore. What happens on Lonsdale, at the Shipyards and along the waterfront determines whether people can build a career here or must commute out of the community to find one.

We’ve seen what focused investment does. The Shipyards revitalization and the arrival of MONOVA and the Polygon Gallery turned the waterfront into a destination — for residents first, and visitors after. Maclean’s recently called this area one of Canada’s coolest neighbourhoods. That didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t happen quickly. It happened because Council committed to a plan and stayed with it.

The same approach works elsewhere. Businesses cluster where there’s a reason to: the Health Innovation District around Lions Gate, marine and technology employment near the waterfront, brewing and food production in the Brewery District. Districts create the density of activity that makes a place worth locating in.

A healthy city also needs healthy people. B.C. will begin licensing psychotherapists in November 2027, and the standards deciding who qualifies are being consulted on this fall. I’ll be making the case that the Province and regulator recognizes the full range of therapeutic approaches, so residents can find qualified care that actually fits their needs.

This term I moved the motions to create the Central Lonsdale Business Improvement Area and to endorse the Lonsdale Great Street Plan. Both essentially were about the same thing: giving our main commercial street the organization and the investment it needs to thrive and compete. I want to finish that work — because who doesn’t want to live in a City where people can shop, walk, work, eat and be inspired by local business, great amenities and arts and culture, without leaving the beautiful North Shore.

Angela Girard is a great Councillor and caring leader in the City. I admire her passion in building a more liveable city for all, and she effectively delivered so by promoting multiculturalism and better mobility options at every opportunity possible. Her vast experience and understanding of small businesses make her a trustworthy advisor and integral part of the business community in parts of the City. Angela is approachable, genuine and always puts others first. I feel so lucky to have known her and wholeheartedly support her to be our Councillor again. — Tony Sun, Owner, Reckless Shipyards eBikes & More, Former Board Member, Lower Lonsdale BIA & North Vancouver Resident

sources.text:
Get rapid transit across the Inlet — a fixed, frequent connection on and off the North Shore is the single biggest change available to us, and it needs to move faster than it is

Keep pressing senior governments and TransLink — the projects that matter most aren’t ours to build, which makes advocacy part of the job, not a substitute for it

Keep the North Shore speaking with one voice — North Shore Connects brings three municipalities and two First Nations governments to the table together, because traffic doesn’t stop at municipal boundaries

Deliver the City’s Mobility Strategy — making the short trips easy to do on foot, by bike or by bus takes cars off the road at the times we’re most congested

Build the All Ages and Abilities bike network — connected, protected routes that an eight-year-old or an eighty-year-old can actually use, not painted lines beside moving traffic. That includes finishing the Eastside Connector , linking Grand Boulevard through the Crosscut Bridge to Casano Drive

Safer streets and sidewalks for everyone — more sidewalks, more marked crossings, better lighting and safer intersections, plus sensible rules for e-bikes and scooters so sidewalks stay safe for people on foot

Back the Safe and Active School Travel Program — better crossings and sidewalks around schools mean fewer cars in the drop-off line, and kids who arrive having moved their bodies and talked to someone

Study the Low Level Road extension and the Highway 1 corridor — evaluate whether an east-west connector relieves Marine Drive, and work with the Province on a long-term plan for the Upper Levels

People here don’t sit in traffic because they want to. They sit in traffic because housing they can afford is somewhere else, and the alternatives to driving aren’t good enough yet. Those two problems are the same problem, and neither gets solved by widening a road.

We have two bridges and a limited number of ways on and off the North Shore. We cannot build our way out of that. The congestion backs up onto City streets, cuts off neighbourhoods near the Second Narrows, and makes it harder for businesses here to hire and keep the people they need.

What we can do is give people real choices — frequent transit, safe bike routes, neighbourhoods where the trip to school or the grocery store doesn’t require a car — so that the road space we have goes further.

Two things that open this year show what that looks like. Translink has extended the R2 RapidBus from Phibbs Exchange through to Metrotown, putting Park Royal within a direct ride of the Expo and Millennium Lines. In August, the Crosscut Bridge opened over Highway 1 — a $17 million project the City built with the Province and TransLink, reconnecting the Loutet and Cedar Village neighbourhoods that the highway separated in the 1960s. Neither of those happened without years of pushing, and North Shore Connects is why the pushing works.

Most of the rest depends on decisions made in Victoria and at TransLink. But there is still plenty the City can do on its own. Safe street design, bike infrastructure, how we manage curb space, and where we allow density are all Council decisions, and I’ve supported the work on all of them — including new rules for the e-bikes and scooters that are now part of how people get around.

The goal is straightforward: spend less of your life in a vehicle and more of it in our community.

Angela Girard is a great Councillor and caring leader in the City. I admire her passion in building a more liveable city for all, and she effectively delivered so by promoting multiculturalism and better mobility options at every opportunity possible. Her vast experience and understanding of small businesses make her a trustworthy advisor and integral part of the business community in parts of the City. Angela is approachable, genuine and always puts others first. I feel so lucky to have known her and wholeheartedly support her to be our Councillor again.

— Tony Sun, Owner, Reckless Shipyards eBikes & More, Former Board Member, Lower Lonsdale BIA & North Vancouver Resident

Tie Tax Relief Directly to Affordability: To qualify for this tax break, landlords must legally commit to protecting current tenants and keeping rents at below-market rates.

The Goal: Give landlords a real financial incentive to modernize and preserve our neighborhood character, rather than demolishing affordable homes for luxury redevelopments.

The city-owned vacant lot on the 100 Block of East 1st Street functions as a de facto neighborhood park, it is currently slated for mixed-use redevelopment. This lot can be permanently converted into an official public park. Preserving this vibrant green space within our high-density core ensures that current and future generations always have a natural place to connect, rest, and play.

Investing in Active Communities: We have an opportunity to expand high-quality, all-weather sports fields to support our growing local teams. Upgrading from gravel to modern all-weather surfaces is a direct, valuable investment in the health, well-being, and active lifestyles of our children and adults

Smart, Liveable Urban Design: Let's maximize our community spaces by encouraging new multi-family developments to build beautiful, functional on-site green areas and community gardens rather than concrete plazas. By integrating these spaces directly into new housing, we enhance urban liveability and provide residents with private, usable outdoor sanctuaries right at home

background.quote: I’ve grown up and lived in North Vancouver all my life, and I’ve witnessed how this community has transformed.
I’m running for City Council because as a son of North Vancouver, I want a future here.

Along the way I became an advocate and leader in the community, an improvisational theatre coach and performing artist, and a culture strategist for an international medical device manufacturer.

positions.quote: That change is only accelerating, and I believe our challenge is to grow while protecting what makes this place our home.

I want to serve our long-term public interest as a councillor who approaches the issues that affect us most by engaging in difficult conversations, building real relationships, and drawing from diverse perspectives.

Our city should responsibly and transparently manage the funds that residents and businesses provide. If we can effectively promote civic literacy more people will engage with city hall proactively and positively. Council must manage difficult financial decisions with our long-term interest in mind. This means incorporating the new community engagement framework into the next council’s strategic plan, following through on the call for a public inquiry into the wastewater treatment plant, and monitoring debt servicing and the health of our reserves.

Our city should support diverse housing that allows young people, seniors, and families to stay in our community and share the same neighbourhoods. It’s not just how many units we need to build, it’s about who we are building them for. The people who live and work here should be able to choose North Vancouver as their home. This means mixed-use density in transit corridors, small-scale multi-unit gentle density in residential neighbourhoods, and increasing non-market housing and tenant protections.

My mother Maribell, my partner Sinéad, and I all continue to make our home here in the City of North Vancouver, despite the fact that we struggle to afford to live here. I am running to make sure that all the folks who have dedicated their lives to this community continue to be able to live and thrive here now and into the future.

Our city should be easy and safe to get around for all our residents, businesses, and commuters. Our major transportation infrastructure isn’t municipal, but the city can help to develop solutions. Whatever our ride we’re all pedestrians with places to be, but we need good options to get us there. This means advocating for the expansion of Bus Rapid Transit, supporting an active transportation network, and providing those who already work here with more options to live here.

Our city’s parks and public spaces should build community and promote wellbeing. They can provide social opportunities through recreation, gathering, and incidental encounters with neighbours. With increasing growth and density our parks and public spaces will be even more important. This means multi-functional, adaptive, and inclusive design. It is also an opportunity to engage local First Nations as partners to develop spaces that reflect the cultural heritage of the land.

Our city is increasingly vulnerable to climate change-related disruption and critical infrastructure failures. We all know what happens when one of our two crossings is compromised for hours, just imagine a week, or a month. Emergency preparedness requires redundancy to ensure our safety and security. This means mitigating climate change with more tree canopy and better drainage, reviewing our emergency management plans, and advocating for a redundant and seismically resilient crossing not for transportation, but for resilient critical infrastructure.

sources.text:
Housing on the North Shore is unaffordable and not feasible – especially for our existing rental population, young professionals and families wanting to live here. Municipal policy must focus on who we are building for and what we are building for. We can target this issue by creating a defining guideline on what is ‘affordable housing’ so policy changes can be made.

When an individual household spends less than 30% of their income on appropriate shelter accommodations.

This definition creates an overarching guideline that tackles the questions of:

It is under the council’s purview to ensure adequate, affordable housing inventory for all. Knowing who and what we are building for can guide council on deciding zoning new developments whether this be non-market, rent-to-own, childcare to senior housing.

We can enact this vision for our current zoning and development practices. Using current policy, we can start this vision by expanding the purpose of the Affordable Housing Reserve Fund to streamlining the City’s Inclusionary Housing Policy to be aligned to what is defined by BC Housing as what is considered to be Rental Affordable.

For new secured market rental developments, I would push to adopt that units should be sold at 30% below average rents in the City calculated by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I would like to expand the amount of units secured to 30% and for new stratified developments, at minimum 10% should be rented at deep discounts or supportive housing levels or equivalent cash-in-lieu. .

Additionally, the City’s Inclusionary Housing Policy only applies to rental and strata developments that are seeking a density bonus. A policy change needs to occur of which our housing policy ensures that this type of housing stock is built and made available in all rental buildings. regardless of density bonus or not.

A PDF is available on the City of North Vancouver site for more details on the Definition of Affordability Updated 2012 .

Creating avenues to transition single-family homes into multi-family lots without losing the essence of the neighbourhood.

Provincial housing pressures have pushed the creation of more housing supply, the city has done some work in bylaw changes inteneded to allow multiplex housing in single-family neighbourhoods. I believe that we need to enact policy changes that encapsulates the City’s vision of a “dense, complete community”. To complete such a vision, the goal of the policy is to reduce dependency on car travel, and put most amenities within a 15 minute walking distance.

While there are policies that allow homeowners on single-family plots to renovate, upgrade and build secondary suites, laneway coach houses, or multi-plexes, there are no policies that both assist and incentivize homeowners to transform and/or re-design their plots. Of course we will need to engage with our senior levels of government to help fund and incentivize homeowners and developers who wish to develop in the City of North Vancouver. But at the current municipal level, there are two ways I believe we can start this process to engage and bring more homeowners into the idea of renovating their single-lots into multiplexes.

First: The current city’s Housing Initiatives Grant is too limiting in scope and too small in incentives for those who wish to help with the affordable housing crisis. I want to expand the Housing Initiatives Grant with more funding and widening the scope to help promote the City’s Inclusionary Housing Needs towards the City’s vision of ‘dense, complete communities.’

Second: Looking to investigate if we can optimize the zoning bylaw to make it easier for homeowners to renovate their home. Obstacles and bureaucracy are clear limiting factors to those seeking to densify their home. One example comes from the Zoning Amendment Bylaw No .9137, that the new Floor Space Ratio (FSR) is limited to roughly 10% more than what is currently permitted. If the allowed space barely exceeds that of one home, it can be argued that more will opt to be build a slightly larger, pricier house rather than multiple, smaller affordable units.

The policy goal of workforce housing is a civic priority aimed at providing affordable, purpose-built rental accommodations for low- to moderate-income essential workers

Whether you are a young parent, a professional fresh out of university or just an individual on the career grind, the price to live on the North Shore is becoming more and more unattainable. Whether you are looking to buy or to rent, the fact that the North Shore leads in having the most expensive housing in all of British Columbia has led many to slowly become priced out of the home that they have grown up and lived in as a kid.

A part of my housing policy goals is the expansion of the City’s Inclusionary Housing Policy to secure more rental and stratified units to become rental affordable. I believe it is time to make policies that help secure and provide housing for working people making low to moderate incomes.

It is time to create a detailed workforce housing policy, aimed towards keeping our workforce from the blue-collar workers, to those in healthcare and childcare, to those in public service, local. As the City continues to build our housing supply, we should dedicate a part of those units (a minimum of 20% units secured) to be set aside for individuals and families earning $30-80,000 per year, with unit-based rent protection in perpetuity, which could become its own specific housing policy or be expanded into the scope of the City’s Inclusionary Housing Policy.

It is time that we acknowledge the North Shore’s need to diversify its housing supply, to acknowledge that the laissez-faire of providng towards private developers and market-based solutions will not solve our housing crisis and to acknowledge that support for these proposals is the first intended step in the direction into proving more housing to our workforce, help reduce the cost of housing and to move the needle towards more proactive, like-minded policies.
sources.title: Housing - Max Lai

sources.text:
The North Shore transit issues aren’t new. The issue has only become more pressing and more prevalant since 2014. The reason for our worsening traffic and congestion issues stems from two main issues that consistently affect North Shore traffic.

One, the North Shore serves as a travel intersection for other communities. Whether you’re travelling, working, moving to and from the Island, moving from North Vancouver to West Vancouver, up to Squamish and Whistler, or between Burnaby, Surrey, or beyond, people commute to, from, or through the North Shore daily.

Two, the North Shore’s notable lack of transit options and alternatives exacerbates our traffic issues. We all know that a single accident can so negatively affect North Shore traffic that it ripples into our local streets and grinds all types of travel to a halt. This issue is only profound because there is only two ways to travel to and from the North Shore. The seabus or transitting across one of our two bridges, Lions Gate or Second Narrows.

To manage our traffic and congestion, council need a proactive policy mindset to plan our current and future infrastructure needs. Planning for and around our current obstacles is the best step forward to deal with traffic needs as our current policy should not be dealing with traffic needs only when it becomes relevant. By the way, our last major transit investment, was the Seabus in 1977.

Current policy should have accountable measures to deliver on our community travel and transportation issues. The city’s Mobility Strategy needs to reflect our current and future transit needs, a reflection that this city needs a detailed plan to implement transportation alternatives that are equally or significantly beneficial and competitive against driving.

Updating the current Mobility Strategy through clear, precise details of North Shore’s Transit Plan for the upcoming 4-8-12 years to showcase a more proactive stance on building for and around our infrastructure issues.

Continuation of the NSTS, ‘North Shore Transportaiton Survey’, to ensure clear and precise reporting on current, deliverable actions, and anticipating future travel needs.

Utilizing senior levels of government and working with other municipal governments to get the transit investment the North Shore needs.

Ensure that there is a plan within the next 10 years that looks into North Shore infrastructure. Specifically looking at the replacement of our two bridges and how we can implement rapid transit systems like Skytrain through such investments

Start the infrastructure groundwork to ensure that more than one BRT can be implemented on the North Shore – Ideas for dedicated BRT lines include utilizing the Lonsdale Corridor or utilizing Highway 1 to get BRTs from Burnaby to Upper Lonsdale.

North Vancouver is growing. I’m running to help ensure daily life gets better as we grow, with the right homes and infrastructure, safe and welcoming neighbourhoods, and a City Hall people can understand and trust.

sources.text:
I grew up on the North Shore, and it has always felt like home.

It’s where I learned to ride a bike, spent time on the trails, watched my parents build a small business, and saw how much a community depends on people quietly showing up for one another.

Today, my wife and I have built our own life here. I’m running for City Council because I care deeply about what North Vancouver becomes next, and I want it to remain a place where people at every stage of life can belong, contribute, and build a future.

My family’s North Vancouver story began more than 30 years ago, when my parents ran a small convenience store near Lonsdale and 15th. I learned from them what it means to work hard, care for your neighbours, and give back to the community that gives you a home.

My mom spent more than 40 years working as a care aide. My wife is a registered nurse. Through them, I’ve seen the dedication behind the public services we depend on, and how difficult it can be for the people who care for our community to afford a life here themselves.

Those experiences shaped how I see North Vancouver. A city is ultimately about people. The families raising kids, neighbours looking out for one another, seniors hoping to stay close to home, people working shifts, and small businesses trying to build something lasting.

As Chair of the City’s Advisory Planning Commission , I spend a lot of time thinking about the choices that shape North Vancouver. Housing, land use, transportation, neighbourhoods, public spaces, and how growth fits into the community around it.

It has taught me to listen carefully, ask difficult questions, and recognize that good decisions rarely come from looking at only one side of an issue.

Professionally, I’ve spent nearly two decades working in strategy, finance, and planning. I’ve worked with large budgets, forecasts, performance, risk, and complex decisions where the numbers matter, but so does understanding the people affected by them.

And I believe good planning includes knowing when to revisit a plan. Circumstances change, and sometimes the right decision is to adjust course. I want City Hall to be clear about what we’re trying to achieve, measure whether it’s working, and be willing to change direction when the evidence tells us we should.

North Vancouver is growing, and the choices we make over the next few years will shape this city for a long time.

I want us to build the homes people need while making sure infrastructure and services keep pace. I want neighbourhoods that feel safe, welcoming, green, and connected. And I want a City Hall that brings people into decisions earlier, explains the trade-offs clearly, and follows through on what it promises.

I’m running because I can contribute something meaningful to that work. A thoughtful approach, strong financial and planning experience, and a genuine desire to listen before making balanced recommendations.

I’ll do my homework, ask hard questions, stay accessible, and be clear about how I’ve reached a decision. And when something isn’t working, I’ll be willing to say so and help find a better way forward.

I chaired the North Vancouver Museum & Archives Commission and City Library Board, and authored North Vancouver’s Lonsdale Neighbourhood, a local history book.

On pay parking, I listened to residents and businesses and advocated for 30-minute free curbside parking and 3-hour free parking at Harry Jerome. I opposed the Swim Deck project after concluding that its cost estimate was conceptual and not sufficiently detailed. I stood up for displaced tenants.

After earning his Bachelor of Science and Executive MBA degrees from Simon Fraser University, Shervin built a successful career in business, technology, and leadership, including as Senior Manager of Technology Planning at TransLink. He later pursued his passion for teaching by becoming a faculty lecturer at Langara College’s School of Management, teaching project management and a range of business courses.

Alongside his full-time professional career, Shervin devoted decades to serving the North Vancouver community. He mentored local teenagers through Family Services of the North Shore, served on the North Vancouver Museum and Archives Commission, including two years as Chair, and authored the frequently cited local history book North Vancouver’s Lonsdale Neighbourhood. He later chaired the North Vancouver City Library Board for five years, and co-organized a Lions Gate Hospital Foundation fundraiser that helped increase cultural safety for Indigenous elders and families while bringing Indigenous art to a North Vancouver long-term care facility.
I have lived in North Vancouver for over 40 years, and I love this City.

In 1984, Albert, a stranger from North Vancouver, changed the course of Shervin’s life. At the time, Shervin was a teenage newcomer to Canada, struggling to find work and gain admission to college. The two met when Albert offered him a ride while Shervin was hitchhiking during the summer-long bus strike.
That chance encounter and Albert’s kindness led to a life-changing college admission, his first job, and it set Shervin on a career path that would ultimately prepare him to serve on City Council.

Shervin Shahriari announces re-election bid for a second term on Council. Click here to view Press Release

In 1984, Albert, a stranger from North Vancouver, changed the course of Shervin’s life. At the time, Shervin was a teenage newcomer to Canada, struggling to find work and gain admission to college. The two met when Albert offered him a ride while Shervin was hitchhiking during the summer-long bus strike. That chance encounter and Albert’s kindness led to a life-changing college admission, his first job, and it set Shervin on a career path that would ultimately prepare him to serve on City Council.

“It all started with Albert taking the time to listen to me and stand up for what he felt was the right thing to do. Ever since, I have tried to live my life by listening to people, understanding what matters to them, and making a positive difference in their lives,” says Shervin.

A background in education and career that serves the role of Councillor

After earning his Bachelor of Science and Executive MBA degrees from Simon Fraser University, Shervin built a successful career in business, technology, and leadership, including as Senior Manager of Technology Planning at TransLink. He later pursued his passion for teaching by becoming a faculty lecturer at Langara College’s School of Management, teaching project management and a range of business courses.

Alongside his full-time professional career, Shervin devoted decades to serving the North Vancouver community. He mentored local teenagers through Family Services of the North Shore, served on the North Vancouver Museum and Archives Commission, including two years as Chair, and authored the frequently cited local history book North Vancouver’s Lonsdale Neighbourhood. He later chaired the North Vancouver City Library Board for five years, and co-organized a Lions Gate Hospital Foundation fundraiser that helped increase cultural safety for Indigenous elders and families while bringing Indigenous art to a North Vancouver long-term care facility. In 2022, Shervin was elected to his first term on City of North Vancouver Council.

“I love North Vancouver. Our city is a wonderful place to live, and being named Canada’s most livable city for two years in a row is something we can all be proud of. But we cannot take that for granted,” says Shervin. “Growth should strengthen our city, not diminish what makes it special, and everyone should share in North Vancouver’s exceptional quality of life. During my first four years on Council, I listened to the community first, thought independently, and stood with residents to preserve what makes North Vancouver special.”

“My approach on Council has been to consider every issue on its own merits. I voted independently, based on the facts before me, and on what I heard from the community. Those principles shaped the way I approached my work throughout my first term on Council.

I supported projects that strengthen our community, including North Shore Neighbourhood House Phase 2, with its respite centre and housing for people who work here; the completion of the Harry Jerome Community Recreation Centre and Silver Harbour Seniors’ Activity centre project, which were already underway when I was elected; new parks and public spaces; improvements to the Shipyards, the library, and the museum; and upgrades to the Mickey McDougall Community Recreation Centre, the new home of Flicka Gymnastics.

Beyond these projects, I successfully championed initiatives to enhance pedestrian safety and walkability, improve accessibility for lowincome people with disabilities across the North Shore, encourage the retention of mature trees, and encourage vibrancy at the street level by managing the proliferation of money service businesses.

I also advocated for safe, practical and accessible active transportation improvements, rapid transit, traffic flow and adequate parking, the preservation of heritage buildings, 30-minute free parking, continued investment in core infrastructure and public assets, and the responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars. I also raised concerns at Council and publicly about the escalating costs of the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant project, its disproportionate financial impact on North Shore taxpayers, and strongly supported calls for an independent public inquiry.

Just as importantly, I opposed proposals when, after listening to the community, I believed they were not in our community’s best interests or when there had not been adequate public consultation. I opposed the Harbour Swimming Deck proposal, seven-day-a-week pay parking from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., aspects of the St. Andrews bike lane design, the closure of sections of West Grand Boulevard, and elements of the Lonsdale Great Street project that required greater clarity and public consultation. I also voted against resolutions related to development proposals when I believed they did not adequately address parking, tenant displacement or when whe I believed the loss of mature trees or a heritage building could have been avoided.

Looking ahead, I will continue to push for practical measures that support responsible growth and preserve the qualities that make North Vancouver such an exceptional place to live. My platform will build on the same principles that have guided my work on Council over the past four years,” says Shervin.

Everyone needs to be able to choose how they move around. Whether you walk, roll, drive or take transit, you should be able to do so safely and responsibly. And it should be fun too!

The City has built new protected mobility corridors, including Esplanade, Crosscut Bridge, and West 1st Street. These projects improve connections with our neighbours and help create a more complete transportation network. This work is not just about bikes. It is about freedom, independence, and accessibility, especially for people with disabilities, seniors, and anyone who uses mobility supports and needs safe, connected routes to move through the city.

There is more to do, and we need to continue working closely with the District of North Vancouver, TransLink, and our regional partners — but we are making real progress. Together with TransLink, we helped bring RapidBus service to the North Shore, supported by dedicated bus lanes that now move thousands of commuters more efficiently every day. The next step is Bus Rapid Transit: a faster, more reliable form of bus service with dedicated lanes, priority at intersections, frequent service, and better stations to move more people without requiring everyone to drive.

Experience here and around the world shows that we cannot simply build our way out of traffic congestion. The only real way to manage traffic is to give people better options. When more people can choose transit, walking, rolling, cycling, or other forms of mobility, our streets work better for everyone — including those who drive. These alternatives to single-occupancy vehicles are not just cheaper, cleaner, and more efficient; they also help make our city healthier, more accessible, and more fun.

Move public transit forward – Bus Rapid Transit creates bus priority to ensure people using transit are rewarded with time and advocate for a new Second Narrows crossing that enables public transit

Vote to create a safe and complete mobility network for all ages that supports transportation choices

Support active living by expanding shared transportation options and supporting improved lighting and sidewalks for pedestrians

By creating more housing options we can ensure more accessible and affordable housing options for all.

The City has made real progress in diversifying the shapes and sizes of homes available in our community. We have focused new housing near major corridors and frequent transit, including areas now supported by RapidBus service. This helps give more people the option to live close to work, school, services, and transportation.

Today, many new rental projects are coming online. Over the last eight years, the City has seen its largest increase in rental homes since the 1970s. I have supported stronger protections for long-time renters and worked to ensure people impacted by redevelopment receive support to relocate and remain connected to their community.

Looking ahead, I will continue to support more purpose-built rental housing, non-market housing, co-operative housing, co-housing, and workforce housing. We need homes for people across incomes — including seniors, youth, families, essential workers, and those most at risk of being pushed out.

We also need to better integrate rental housing with local commercial areas, including retail and office developments. The most vibrant and livable cities in the world combine homes, shops, services, public spaces, and transit so people can meet more of their daily needs close to home.

Housing is about more than buildings. It is about whether people can build a life here, stay connected to their community, and see a future for themselves in the City of North Vancouver.

Create more housing options in the right places by focusing new homes near frequent transit, services, shops, schools, and public spaces — while ensuring development contributes fairly to community amenities.

Support more affordable and non-market housing by expanding co-op, social, co-housing, workforce, and non-market options through federal and provincial funding, partnerships, and municipal tools.

Protect people through change by strengthening renter protections, supporting residents through redevelopment, and prioritizing long-time residents, seniors, youth, workers, and vulnerable households

Managing and expanding municipal assets that ensure our quality of life is essential. The majority of our population lives in multi-family buildings without lots of outdoor spaces, so supporting public spaces is critical to enjoying our city and enhancing community connections.

When people live in apartments, condos, co-ops, and townhomes, shared public spaces become even more important. Parks, plazas, playgrounds, dog parks, street trees, sidewalks, mobility routes, sports courts, community facilities, and welcoming streets all become part of people’s everyday living space.

That is why I will continue to support investments in infrastructure and public spaces that serve the vast majority of our residents. Great public spaces help make compact living more livable, support mental and physical health, create opportunities for fitness and social connection, and strengthen the North Shore lifestyle we all value.

Public spaces also support local businesses and our local economy. When people have great places to gather, walk, shop, eat, play, and spend time, our commercial areas become more vibrant and resilient.

I have supported initiatives to expand public amenities across the city, including new parklets, more dog parks, expanded street tree coverage, improved active transportation connections, and new skate park facilities.

A more affordable city must also be a more livable city. That means building homes, but also investing in the public spaces and infrastructure that allow people to thrive.

Create greener, better-connected neighbourhoods by protecting mature trees, expanding street tree coverage, securing more green space through development, and supporting green mid-block pedestrian connectors, pocket parks, and improved access to transit.

Invest in accessible, people-focused public spaces with washrooms, seating, shade, trees, play areas, dog spaces, parklets, outdoor art, and gathering places that work for people of all ages and abilities.

Protect quality of life as the city grows by managing urban noise, addressing impacts from landscaping equipment, modified vehicle exhausts, and construction, while securing access to important recreation amenities like tennis and pickleball courts.

Expand small-scale public spaces across the city through parklets, barklets, dog runs, pocket parks, outdoor art, and better pedestrian connections that make dense neighbourhoods feel more livable, social, and green.

Championing small businesses, local entrepreneurs, and nationally significant employers, so our city remains vibrant, diverse, and prosperous.

A strong local economy means a stronger North Vancouver. When more people can work, shop, access services, and run businesses close to home, we reduce pressure on our transportation network and give people back more time with family, friends, and community.

Our economy is diverse and more significant than many people realize. Alongside our growing health-care sector, North Vancouver is home to major employers and nationally significant companies connected to the port, trade, marine, industrial, and export sectors. These businesses provide good local jobs, support regional supply chains, and play an important role in Canada’s economy — especially at a time when the country is under pressure to strengthen productivity, trade, infrastructure, and economic resilience.

Many small and family-run businesses are under real pressure. They are struggling to find workers, manage rising costs, and absorb high property taxes. This is where housing affordability, transportation, public space, and economic sustainability all come together. If people who work in North Vancouver cannot afford to live here — or cannot get here efficiently — local businesses, services, and institutions all feel the impact. That is why we need to advance workforce housing, improve transportation options, and continue investing in vibrant streets, plazas, patios, parklets, markets, events, and welcoming commercial areas that bring people together and support the foot traffic small businesses depend on.

The City’s updated 2024 Economic Strategy gives us a stronger framework to support this work, with a focus on strengthening employment lands, making it easier to do business, creating world-class public places, and building a resilient local economy. It also identifies opportunities to grow the health and innovation cluster around Lions Gate Hospital and revitalize Central Lonsdale as a destination for community and commercial activity. The creation of the Central Lonsdale Business Improvement Area is an important step, giving local businesses and property owners a stronger collective voice to support events, beautification, marketing, safety, and economic vitality in one of the City’s most important commercial districts.

Advocate for fairer business taxation so small businesses are not unfairly burdened by property taxes based on the “highest and best use” of land.

Build on our economic strengths by supporting health and innovation around Lions Gate Hospital, film and creative industries in Bridgman, and the port, marine, trade, and export sectors.

Advance workforce housing so more people who work in North Vancouver can afford to live here.

Support vibrant commercial districts through business improvement associations, better public spaces, patios, parklets, events, and welcoming streets.

Improve goods movement by exploring logistics hubs and practical solutions that reduce congestion while supporting local businesses.

sources.text:
Linda was first elected Mayor of the City of North Vancouver in November, 2018. Her goal is to build a healthy and inclusive city where people come first.

As Mayor, she has established herself as a leader both on the North Shore and throughout Metro Vancouver. She is proud to serve as Chair of Metro Vancouver’s Invest Vancouver Management Board as well as a member of the TransLink Mayors’ Council on Regional Transportation where she is Chair of the Public Affairs and Governance Standing Committee. As a member of the TransLink Mayors’ Council and Chair of North Shore Connects, she has led the charge to secure rapid transit to the North Shore.

Prior to her election as Mayor, Linda served as a member of North Vancouver City Council from 2011 to 2018 and prior to that she was an elected Trustee on the North Vancouver School Board.

Born and raised in the City, Linda has deep roots in North Vancouver. Her father, Jim Buchanan, was a popular teacher and principal whose name is given to the annual “Buchanan Bowl” football match between Carson Graham and Handsworth high schools and the James Buchanan Theatre at Argyle secondary school. Her mother, Verna, has served the community in a volunteer capacity for decades. Linda credits her parents for her love for the community and public service.

Linda holds a Bachelor’s Degree with Honours in nursing from the University of British Columbia. Prior to her election as Mayor, Linda worked for close to 30 years as a public health nurse for Vancouver Coastal Health delivering preventative nursing services and immunization programs to the general public, members of the Squamish Nation, and in North Shore schools and community clinics. In 2019, she received the UBC School of Nursing Centenary Medal of Distinction for her achievements in nursing and in 2023 she received the UBC Faculty of Applied Science Dean’s Medal of Distinction for excellence in her field.

Linda’s first involvement in civic politics came through her role in helping to secure funding for the heritage preservation and renovation of Ridgeway Elementary School, one of the City’s most important heritage properties. She is a founding member of the Ridgeway Heritage Society.

Linda lives in the Ridgeway/Grand Boulevard neighbourhood with her husband, Kevin, where they raised their four children. They enjoy riding their bikes along the Spirit Trail, listening to jazz music, and supporting the local arts and culture scene.

Better City services. Housing that fits people’s lives. Practical action to make it easier to get around.

The campaign now has a complete seven-part platform. Each area begins with a clear commitment and keeps the supporting detail available for people who want to look deeper.

Local government should make everyday life easier to navigate—and be candid about how well it is performing.

Tell people what to expect from City Hall, measure performance and publish the results.

Plan housing, transportation, parks and services around how people actually live.

Explain the tradeoffs, show what changed and take responsibility for the outcome.

Dave Kurvers has spent more than three decades working in British Columbia’s film and television industry, where planning, coordination and solving complex problems are part of the job.

His background also includes public-policy leadership, service on Elections BC’s Election Advisory Committee, and university study in human and economic geography and business administration.

Dave is running for Mayor to make City Hall more responsive, accountable and focused on results for North Vancouver residents and businesses.

A municipal campaign grows through neighbours who contribute, volunteer and show their support. Choose the way you would like to help.

Help fund voter outreach, campaign materials and the work of sharing a practical plan for North Vancouver.

Help with events, canvassing, community outreach and the practical work of a citywide campaign.

Request a lawn sign for your home or business when campaign sign distribution begins.

The campaign’s contribution and sign-up forms are being prepared. They will be activated here once the campaign details and destination links are confirmed.

Follow Dave for campaign news, new policy detail and opportunities to get involved.

Each section begins with a clear commitment and keeps the implementation detail available for people who want to look deeper.

Clear service standards, productive administration, responsible budgets and public accountability for major projects.

Business retention, faster approvals, measurable local-business health and commercial streets that work.

Homes with enough space, useful layouts, secure tenure and options for different stages of life.

Transportation ideas that fit North Vancouver, reliable access and better local and regional connections.

Meaningful choices before major planning decisions, protected public land and infrastructure alongside growth.

More useful shared space, disciplined recreation projects and public places designed for everyday community life.

The right response from the right service, accessibility from the beginning and practical relationships that deliver results.

For an application that is complete, compliant and within the City’s portion of the process.

Where the use is permitted and all City requirements have been satisfied.

sources.text:
Clear requirements, published service standards, productive administration, resilient budgets and public accountability for major projects.

These standards apply when an application is complete and compliant. They cover the City’s portion of the process and do not waive provincial health, liquor, fire, building, safety or other legal requirements.

Straightforward applications that are complete and compliant.

Where the use is permitted and all City requirements are satisfied.

Publish a complete checklist before an applicant spends money.

Run internal reviews in parallel where possible rather than serially.

Publish the percentage of files meeting the service standard.

Identify repeat-review causes and fix the workflow rather than normalizing rework.

If we don’t measure how City Hall performs, we can’t manage it or improve it.

Use machines for repetitive work. Use people for judgment and public service.

Automation and AI can help with permit completeness checks, routine zoning and document pre-checks, missing-material detection, workflow routing, status communication and searches of internal technical information.

Benchmark Development Services using turnaround time, files completed per staff member, cost per application, repeat review cycles, customer feedback and the percentage of applications meeting service standards.

Review whether permit fees can fall as the cost per file falls

Important distinction: permit and application fees support administration. Growth-related infrastructure charges should not become a substitute for an inefficient permitting bureaucracy.

Can City Hall balance the books if development slows for three years?

Before approving each five-year financial plan, publish a normal case, a slow-growth case and a severe-slowdown case.

Materially lower permit activity, development revenue and tax-base growth for three years.

A prolonged downturn without assuming reserves can cover the gap indefinitely.

Temporary growth revenue should not create permanent spending problems.

Major City projects should have one public record that preserves the complete cost, schedule, scope and financing history.

Also required for significant municipal debt or the sale or long-term lease of strategic City land.

Triggered by a cost increase above 20 percent, a delay beyond six months, or a material change in scope or financing.

If the cost, schedule, scope or financing changes materially, show the public what changed before simply moving on.

Keep annual tax increases close to inflation where practical.

Show the real dollar effect on representative households and businesses.

Separate ongoing revenue from one-time or growth-related revenue.

Show which operating costs are growing faster than inflation and why.

Direct unexpected development or assessment growth first toward reserves, infrastructure, debt reduction or tax stabilization before creating permanent commitments.

The goal is simple: a City government we can afford in good years and slower ones.

Strengthen disclosure expectations for elected officials and senior staff, particularly around development, procurement and significant land transactions.

Stronger public reporting around development, procurement and significant land transactions

A culture where conflicts are declared before controversy arises
