sources.text:
New investment is welcome, but the City should first make sure businesses already here can survive, expand and reinvest.

A complete, straightforward business-licence application should receive a City decision within one week. Commercial tenant improvements should also have published service standards.

Carry forward lawful approvals and infrastructure when a new business takes over substantially the same use, wherever legally possible.

A City that says it is open for business should be able to show how long it takes to open one.

City delay has a cost, even when it never appears in the City budget.

A business can burn rent, wages and working capital while waiting for approvals. City reporting should show where delay occurs and how often applicants must repeat work.

Measure the tradeoffs before and after changing a commercial street.

Before major changes to parking, loading, vehicle access, curb allocation, streetscape design or prolonged construction, publish a short business-impact assessment. After implementation, measure what actually happened.

A business-impact review does not automatically veto a transportation or public-space project. It ensures Council sees the tradeoffs beforehand and the results afterward.

Before City Hall changes access to a commercial street, it should know what businesses depend on that access and measure what happens afterward.

Publish a clear picture of whether local businesses are thriving or being displaced.

The City should publish a full Local Business Health Report annually, supported by quarterly service and permitting measures.

Encourage small, adaptable commercial units and narrow storefronts where appropriate.

Use stable and transparent terms in City-owned commercial premises.

Explore relocation or return opportunities for established businesses displaced by redevelopment.

Evaluate lawful provincial tax-relief tools where appropriate.

Advocate for better commercial-lease disclosure and transparency.

The City cannot impose residential-style rent controls on private commercial leases.

Spread more of the Shipyards’ energy through Lonsdale and selected commercial areas without defining vibrancy as alcohol-oriented nightlife.

Evening cafes, restaurants, dessert shops and independent retail

Practical location and noise rules that protect nearby residents

On selected side streets, consider housing above small flexible commercial spaces. Do not impose ground-floor commercial where demand will not support it.

Give visitors reasons to explore Lower and Central Lonsdale and other commercial areas.

Support resident-hosted visitor accommodation where it does not remove ordinary long-term rental housing.

The objective is more visitor spending in local businesses without worsening housing availability for residents.

Measure housing success by affordability and suitability, not simply by unit count.

Build homes people can actually live in through different stages of life.

We’re building much smaller homes on much less land, but the price isn’t falling by much.

Use modern building forms to create better family apartments.

Support single-egress-stair and other modern building forms where provincial rules permit them, to create better apartment layouts for families.

Genuine family apartments rather than relying only on rowhouses

Redevelopment should not price people out of their own neighbourhood.

Interim housing assistance or rent top-up while rebuilding occurs

Make good housing projects possible and bring the right partners together.

Support social, non-market, supportive and Indigenous-led housing through senior-government partnerships, established providers and practical municipal coordination.

Partnerships with non-profit and Indigenous housing providers

The City should not default to selling public land to deliver housing.

Help residents remain connected to their community as their needs change.

Practical City processes for accessibility changes, secondary suites and shared family property arrangements

A clear early checklist so families can confirm ownership and consent requirements before spending heavily

Proportionate rules for short, low-impact activities such as temporary material delivery

sources.text:
Regional rapid transit and local North Shore movement are related, but they are not the same problem.

TransLink connects us to the region. A North Shore network should move us around the North Shore.

This is not opposition to rapid transit. The concern is whether large elevated guideways fit the terrain, neighbourhoods and dispersed travel patterns of the North Shore. Regional transit can connect to the North Shore, with passengers transferring into a local network designed for local destinations.

Whether one regional line serves dispersed North Shore trips

Let qualified proponents develop the project. Make the City an effective enabler.

Encourage qualified private proponents, investors, landowners, manufacturers and operating groups to bring forward proposals to finance, design, build, operate and maintain a North Shore ropeway network. Start with one technically and commercially viable corridor.

Prefer private financing and private responsibility for construction and operations. Assess proposals before determining whether public support is needed.

The private sector can develop the project. The City should make sure a good project can actually get built.

Make the Quay the gateway between Metro Vancouver and the Sea-to-Sky corridor.

Protect the opportunity for a future passenger rail station and access while integrating the waterfront with SeaBus, buses, regional rapid transit, North Shore ropeways, walking and cycling.

Protect station and access opportunities in land-use planning.

Avoid waterfront decisions that foreclose future rail access.

Plan the Quay as one multimodal node rather than disconnected terminals.

Service details and timing would depend on corridor engineering and a viable business case.

The objective should not be maximum parking or minimum parking. It should be reliable access.

Encourage realistic off-street parking, especially for larger family homes, within provincial law.

Encourage shared or dedicated garages serving multiple buildings or commercial areas.

Prioritize curb space for short-term access, customers, visitors, accessible parking, trades, loading, deliveries and pickups.

Measure occupancy, turnover, accessibility, customer experience and business effects.

Parking should support community life, not get in the way of it.

Your first interaction with a neighbourhood should not be a parking app.

Keep the existing short free period straightforward and visible.

Consider merchant validation and pay-on-exit in appropriate City lots.

Measure user difficulty and abandoned transactions, not only occupancy.

People should not be penalized for the vehicle their job requires.

Develop a practical policy or permit for resident work vehicles that can be parked safely without blocking sidewalks, driveways, sightlines, loading or emergency access.

Plan off-street hubs where shared vehicles can park, charge, clean and wait.

Provide managed pickup and drop-off space at major destinations.

Design new parking structures so they can be converted if demand changes.

Do not assume a specific deployment date for autonomous fleets.

A good sidewalk moves people. A great sidewalk also gives people a reason to stay.

sources.text:
My door is open. Rebuilding trust starts with showing up and listening. That's why I'll hold regular Meet the Mayor events: open, unscripted, where residents can ask hard questions and get straight answers. You shouldn't need an appointment or a connection to talk to your mayor. Residents won't wait a year to hear from me directly: I'll deliver a free, public State of the City address within my first six to eight months.

That number isn't apathy. It's a lot of people who've concluded their voice doesn't matter at City Hall, and I think they have a point. Too often, "public engagement" means being brought in only after the plan is already decided - a survey to check a box, not a real chance to change anything. Not every decision needs a public vote, but residents deserve real debate while a decision can still move, not a rubber stamp once it can't.

We're being forced to shoulder more than our fair share of the cost overruns at the wastewater plant, under a regional cost-sharing formula that loads a heavier tax burden onto North Shore residents than the rest of the region. Costs keep climbing, and even after two rounds of letters and votes demanding independent oversight, the cost-sharing formula still hasn't changed.

It's not just the wastewater plant. Five years ago, City Hall had essentially no debt; today it's authorized roughly $165 million in borrowing for Harry Jerome and the North Shore Neighbourhood House alone, on top of our share of a wastewater plant where the North Shore covers 37% of the cost despite being 8% of the region's population. Worthwhile projects can still come with real financial risk, and residents deserve a mayor who's straight with them about what's already committed, and what still needs to be worked out, before signing off on the next one.

The province requires some density near transit, and that's fair. What wasn't required: a density transfer that pushed a 21-storey tower onto an East 14th Street block the OCP itself capped at 6 to 8, or restricting residents to written comments only, a step beyond what the province's own rules require. It's one example among several of decisions getting made without residents at the table. As Capilano Mall, the ICBC lands, and Lonsdale Great Street move forward, that's the standard I'll hold to.

Growth done right should also mean growth the city can actually move around. I want real capacity for walking, cycling, and transit alongside the roads we still rely on, built in from the start, not bolted on after the gridlock arrives. This is the city I love: mountains, ocean, and trails minutes from downtown, a place worth getting right as it grows.

Today’s decisions should work for every generation and make it possible for the next one to build a life and stay in North Vancouver.

You don't have to wait until I'm elected. Ask me something now.
sources.title: Priorities | McGraw for Mayor

North Vancouver has always been home. I am a lifelong resident of the District and have been proud to serve on Council since 2018. I live in Lynn Valley with my wife, Signy, and our two young kids.

Professionally, I have spent more than 20 years working in advertising and sales and hold a Bachelor of Music from UBC. During my time on Council, I have also served on a number of community boards and committees, including the Library Board, Museum and Archives Commission, and the District’s Climate Action Advisory Committee. I am running as an independent candidate and will continue to approach each issue on its merits, listen carefully to residents and work collaboratively to find practical solutions.

If re-elected, my priorities include improving how we move around the North Shore through better transit, safer walking and cycling connections, and strong advocacy for replacement of the Ironworkers Memorial Bridge. I will continue supporting thoughtful housing choices that help young people, families and seniors remain in our community, with most growth focused near town centres, transit, shops and services. I also want to advance financially responsible plans to renew aging community facilities, protect our parks, trails and natural environment, prepare for climate risks, and continue pushing for transparency and accountability at Metro Vancouver.

My goal is a connected, sustainable and welcoming North Vancouver where people of every generation can build a life and feel heard.

background.quote: I bring the experience of serving two terms on District Council, a record of community volunteering and nonprofit leadership, and more than 15 years as a professional engineer working on major transportation infrastructure.

In 2014, District residents elected me to Council, and I served two terms through 2022. My roles included serving as alternate to the TransLink Mayors’ Council, Council liaison to the Major Infrastructure Projects Advisory Committee and Heritage Advisory Committee, and a member of the Finance and Audit Committee and Metro Vancouver Housing Committee. I advocated for affordable housing partnerships, safer active transportation and open, accountable public decision-making. That experience taught me what local government can accomplish, where it depends on partnerships, and how much good decisions rely on listening, preparation and clear priorities.

My career has included work in both the private and public sectors. For the first ten years of my engineering career, I travelled across British Columbia, working on complex transportation problems and implementing practical solutions. In 2018, I stepped away from full-time engineering to focus on caring for my young children. During that time, I balanced parenting with consulting engineering, bicycle courier work, community volunteering and service as treasurer of the Lynn Valley Parent Participation Preschool. In 2022, I returned to full-time engineering work.

From 2008 to 2013, I served as president of the North Shore Mountain Bike Association. During that time, a volunteer group with more work than time or money grew into an organization with paid staff, strong partnerships with businesses and local governments, and an engaged membership. My role was to help set a clear direction, build the team and nurture the relationships needed to get things done.
I also know what it means to choose North Vancouver, work to find a suitable home, raise my two children here and manage the everyday cost of living in this community.

My parents moved from Ontario to the Lower Mainland and built a home-renovation business during the difficult economy of the early 1980s, a business they still run today. As a child, I travelled with my mom as she picked up cheques, paid bills and signed contracts, and I spent time working with my dad on job sites around Metro Vancouver.

I graduated from Simon Fraser University in 2008 with a Bachelor of Applied Science in Systems Engineering and a Certificate in Sustainable Community Development. I carried a full-time engineering course load, maintained the grades needed for a scholarship and worked part time to pay my way through university without a student loan.

positions.quote: Infrastructure, transportation, public facilities and services shape daily life in North Vancouver. The District must maintain what people rely on, plan ahead and invest with a clear understanding of long-term value and cost.
I am running again because the District faces major decisions about infrastructure, transportation and long-term costs.

District residents are paying hundreds of millions of dollars for the over-runs at Metro Vancouver's Wastewater Treatment Plant. We cannot allow failures on that scale to happen again. We must invest responsibly in infrastructure, transportation, public facilities and services to maintain and improve the quality of life we've all come to enjoy.

Major capital projects need careful oversight and clear accountability. Council must understand costs and risks, test assumptions, demand clear reporting and explain the consequences to residents.

Infrastructure, transportation, public facilities and services shape daily life in North Vancouver.

We must maintain and improve infrastructure, transportation and the services people rely on, while understanding long-term costs and demanding accountability for major projects.

Council is strongest when members each bring their different experience to the table and test decisions from more than one perspective.
I do not pretend to have every answer. I try to listen carefully, ask practical questions and clearly explain the trade-offs in the decisions before us.
Affordability and quality of life belong in the same conversation. People at every stage of life should be able to build roots, stay connected and see a future in North Vancouver.

A District for all to thrive for generations to come. That vision has inspired my public service since I was first elected in 2014.

Our neighbours, friends and families should be able to build roots, stay connected and see their future here at every stage of life. The next Council will make tough decisions about affordability and quality of life that will shape our community for generations. We must maintain and improve infrastructure, transportation and the services people rely on, while understanding long-term costs and demanding accountability for major projects.

Council is strongest when members each bring their different experience to the table and test decisions from more than one perspective. I bring the experience of serving two terms on District Council, a record of community volunteering and nonprofit leadership, and more than 15 years as a professional engineer working on major transportation infrastructure. I understand how local government works, where partnerships are needed and how Council decisions shape our community.

I also know what it means to choose North Vancouver, work to find a suitable home, raise my two children here and manage the everyday cost of living in this community. Together, these experiences help me bring people together, work through complex problems and keep Council decisions grounded in how they affect daily life.

I am running again to help Council make responsible decisions, protect what we value about North Vancouver and keep building a community where we can all make a good life.

My approach to public service was shaped long before I entered politics. My parents moved from Ontario to the Lower Mainland and built a home-renovation business during the difficult economy of the early 1980s, a business they still run today. As a child, I travelled with my mom as she picked up cheques, paid bills and signed contracts, and I spent time working with my dad on job sites around Metro Vancouver. Their hard work, dedication and determination shaped my character and taught me what it takes to build something that lasts.

I graduated from Simon Fraser University in 2008 with a Bachelor of Applied Science in Systems Engineering and a Certificate in Sustainable Community Development. I carried a full-time engineering course load, maintained the grades needed for a scholarship and worked part time to pay my way through university without a student loan.

My career has included work in both the private and public sectors. For the first ten years of my engineering career, I travelled across British Columbia, working on complex transportation problems and implementing practical solutions. In 2018, I stepped away from full-time engineering to focus on caring for my young children. During that time, I balanced parenting with consulting engineering, bicycle courier work, community volunteering and service as treasurer of the Lynn Valley Parent Participation Preschool. In 2022, I returned to full-time engineering work. My career now spans more than 15 years and includes major transportation infrastructure projects.

Throughout my career, I have kept learning through formal training and by looking at how other communities tackle transportation, land use, housing, sustainability and climate change. That work has taught me to connect the different parts of a problem, test assumptions, identify risks early and follow decisions through to implementation. It has also reinforced my duty as an engineer to put public safety, health, welfare and the natural environment first.

I believe in service and giving back to the community. From 2008 to 2013, I served as president of the North Shore Mountain Bike Association. During that time, a volunteer group with more work than time or money grew into an organization with paid staff, strong partnerships with businesses and local governments, and an engaged membership. My role was to help set a clear direction, build the team and nurture the relationships needed to get things done. I am proud that successive boards and staff have continued to grow the organization.

In 2014, District residents elected me to Council, and I served two terms through 2022. My roles included serving as alternate to the TransLink Mayors’ Council, Council liaison to the Major Infrastructure Projects Advisory Committee and Heritage Advisory Committee, and a member of the Finance and Audit Committee and Metro Vancouver Housing Committee. I advocated for affordable housing partnerships, safer active transportation and open, accountable public decision-making. That experience taught me what local government can accomplish, where it depends on partnerships, and how much good decisions rely on listening, preparation and clear priorities.

I do not pretend to have every answer. I try to listen carefully, ask practical questions and clearly explain the trade-offs in the decisions before us. I am running again because the District faces major decisions about infrastructure, transportation and long-term costs. I want to bring my experience, passion and grounded way of working back to the Council table.

You can donate, volunteer or request a sign to help the campaign reach more neighbours across the District.

sources.text:
Most campaigns lead with promises. I want to lead with a standard, because the promises only mean something if you know how I'll actually behave once the cameras are off and the hard votes come up.

Good governance isn't complicated. Show up. Have a plan. Be honest. Do what you said you'd do. That's the job. It's easy to say and harder to live up to, which is exactly why it's worth putting in writing before you've given me your vote rather than after.

This page is about the kind of councillor I intend to be. It is not a list of promises. Promises are specific, they can be checked, and they belong on the Commitments page where you can hold me to them.

What follows is the part that comes before that. How I will show up, how I will decide, and what I will tell you when I get something wrong.

Residents deserve leadership that listens and is present, not just in the weeks before an election. Too many decisions get made without most people ever hearing about them until the outcome is already set.

I'll be at the table, in the community, and reachable in between. That includes making a real effort to reach the people councils usually talk past: renters, younger families, and residents like me who will live longest with the choices this council makes. If a decision is going to shape the District for thirty years, the people who'll be here in thirty years deserve a say in it.

Good intentions don't fix aging infrastructure, and they don't bring down the cost of living here. The work is in the details, and the details take homework.

I come to the table prepared. I read the budgets, I dug into the files, and I will bring forward ideas that hold up to scrutiny rather than ones that just sound good in a headline. I'd rather show up with a workable idea and get told no than show up with nothing. And I'll be honest about what one councillor among seven can and can't deliver, because a plan that oversells itself isn't a plan, it's a pitch.

Trust starts with clear communication and open budgets, even when the news is hard. You can't trust a council that only tells you the easy half of the story.

That means plain language instead of process jargon, real numbers instead of reassurance, and a straight answer when the answer is difficult. When I don't know something, I'll say so. When I get something wrong, I'll own it. The goal isn't to look right, it's to give residents an accurate picture of where things actually stand so you can hold your council to it.

Accountability isn't a slogan. It only counts if you can check it.

So I'll publish my voting record and keep it public, so you can measure my choices against the commitments I made to earn your vote. If I said I'd push for something and then voted the other way, you should be able to see that plainly and ask me why. That's the one promise I can keep entirely on my own, without needing four other votes to get there, and I intend to keep it.

A note on transparency. This page has evolved as the campaign has grown. If you'd like to see where it started, the earlier version of my core values is still public here . Nothing disappears, nothing gets quietly edited.

background.quote: I have served on the Social Planning Advisory Council (SPAC) with the City Council, where I helped advise on grants supporting non-profit organizations and community initiatives.
My professional and volunteer experiences have taken me across different fields, including project management, technology and education, as well as local and international community service.
Through my work in finance and education, as well as volunteering locally and internationally, I’ve learned the importance of listening, bringing people together, and making thoughtful decisions.
I have also organized shoreline cleanups and electronic recycling campaigns and volunteered with families navigating times of transition.
I am a passionate community member who is deeply grateful to call Lynn Creek home. My family and I chose North Vancouver because we found a place where we can put down roots for generations to come.

My family and I moved to North Vancouver from Winnipeg, and we quickly knew we had found somewhere special. Today, we’re grateful to call Lynn Creek home and to be building our family and future here.

positions.quote:
You rent while putting money away, hoping that one day—not too far from now—you’ll have enough for a down payment and won’t have to look far to find a home you can afford. You’ll be able to stay right here in the District of North Vancouver.

I think about this often as I watch friends and family move to places they can afford, even when their first choice would be to stay here—to build their lives here, raise their families here, and eventually retire here.

I’m running because I want our children and future generations to have the freedom to choose whether they stay here—not be forced to leave because of affordability, transportation, or lack of opportunity.

We can do better. We can be: thoughtful about growth, creative about affordability, and intentional about building a connected community.

Our family relies on public transit to get around, and we’re also members of our local Modo car co-op—which we love. For us, it works.

But I also understand that every family is different. Work schedules, young children, mobility needs, caregiving responsibilities and other realities can make it difficult to rely on transit or a car-share for every trip.

I’m running for District Councillor because I believe North Vancouver is changing, and I want to help us prepare thoughtfully for what comes next while preserving what makes this community special. I care about housing that allows people to put down roots, transportation that works for everyday life, strong neighbourhood connections, responsible growth, environmental stewardship, and preparing our community for climate and technological change.

I believe progress and preservation don’t have to be opposites.

To honour the choice of numerous families, we must maintain and improve the structures, systems, services and community rhythms that make the District of North Vancouver such a wonderful place to live, while also being willing to look ahead and thoughtfully prepare for the future.

Progress and preservation don’t have to be opposites. We can plan for growth while protecting what matters. We can welcome new neighbours while strengthening the community we already love. And we can make decisions today that ensure North Vancouver remains a place where families can thrive for generations to come. I am committed to:
Good local government means listening with curiosity, asking thoughtful questions, working with others and planning proactively—not reactively.

One of the biggest changes on the horizon is artificial intelligence.

AI is already changing how we work, how we learn, how businesses operate and how we interact with the world around us. As the technology continues to develop, it will increasingly touch many aspects of everyday life—including how we access information, services and opportunities in our community.

Our local government should be thoughtful and proactive, not reactive.

Expanding active transportation networks to keep people moving

I’m proud to be a union member and I believe in the power of union labour.

Increasing availability of affordable housing so workers can live in the community they build rather than commute long distances

Sports & recreation are such an important part of the community. However, access to facilities like ice rinks and pools can be difficult, and this limits the number of people who can participate.

Expanding access to sports facilities so more people can join in

Ensuring that recreation opportunities remain affordable for everyone

Supporting sports organizations and federations to host more competitions in the District

I want a strong relationship with Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw and səlilwətaɬ. I cannot represent a municipality without recognizing how that land came to be and how colonialism continues to harm Indigenous communities. Reconciliation is a verb and I am committed to that work.

The ongoing climate crisis is a real threat. On a municipal level, we see an increasing risk of wildfires in interface areas, increasing drought, increasingly destructive atmospheric rivers. Municipal decisions must be made with robust environmental protections at front of mind. A greener future also means holding the drivers of climate change to account.

The District of North Vancouver should be safe and welcoming for everyone, no matter where you’re from, what language you speak, who you love, what faith your practice, how much money you make, or how a disability might impact your life. I’ve fought for inclusion for years and this work continues!

I was born and raised in Prince George, BC and spent several summers living in Wells, BC. I turned a degree in Political Science and International Studies and a background in writing into a 17-year career in mental health literacy and knowledge translation within the mental health and substance use sector. Through this work, I see first-hand how policy decisions impact individuals and their families and how the right community supports change lives. I’ve been an activist around the Lower Mainland for many years. I continue to research and discuss right-wing extremism in BC, but I’ve centred my activism in my own community. In 2023, a Thursday afternoon Freedom Convoy rally on Mountain Highway overpass began to attack 2SLGBTQIA+ rights. I stood on that overpass almost every Thursday for a year and half. I fought for action from the District of North Vancouver and the Province. I co-authored the North Shore Anti-Hate Pledge, which was endorsed by the District of North Vancouver in 2025. Now I am running for Council for the opportunity to do more.

Click on the articles below for a selection of my words and initiative in the news.

A campaign for accountable government, practical solutions, and a stronger District of North Vancouver.

Written and signed by Graham Gordon Alexander Aguilar, this letter calls for lawful, evidence-based review of concerns about public accountability and alleged wrongdoing.

Publication of this letter records the campaign's correspondence. It does not confirm receipt, a response, personal contact, friendship, endorsement, or support by President Trump or any other person named in the letter.

Read Graham Alexander's candidate profile, prepared for publication in the North Shore News , to learn about his experience and plan for DNV.

Graham Alexander brings energy, creativity, and fun to the campaign for Mayor of the District of North Vancouver.

Filmed on Hollywood Boulevard alongside costumed Spider-Man, Batman, and Marilyn Monroe performers, Take Me Home Tonight shows Graham's lighter side. He is a candidate who will bring more fun to DNV.

The debate begins at 7:00 PM. Please allow extra time to arrive and find a seat.

Graham Alexander will participate in the Edgemont all-candidates debate.

The campaign states that Prime Minister Mark Carney and Braeden Caley are expected to attend. Attendance, speaking arrangements, and any endorsement or other participation require confirmation by the debate organizer, the Prime Minister's Office, the individuals, or an official campaign statement.

Residents should not be left paying for unexplained infrastructure cost escalation. Graham is calling for transparent, independent accounting of reported wastewater-project costs, including the reported rise from approximately $700 million to $4 billion.

As Mayor, Graham will fight for a forensic review, public records, and every lawful avenue to recover public funds where losses or misconduct are established. Any claim, recovery, or compensation depends on the evidence and the outcome of the proper legal process.

Read Graham's professional background, engineering experience, and platform for the District of North Vancouver in an article prepared for publication in the North Shore News .

If you are a District of North Vancouver resident, register for campaign legal-accountability updates and follow-up.

The campaign legal team will receive your registration and email you a confirmation. Registration is not a court filing and does not guarantee compensation or any legal outcome.

Watch Graham's three-minute summary of the campaign and the practical solutions DNV needs.

Graham Alexander will participate in the October 8 all-candidates debate in Edgemont.

The campaign has stated that Prime Minister Mark Carney and Braeden Caley are expected to attend. Attendance, speaking arrangements, and any endorsement or other participation must be confirmed by the debate organizer, the Prime Minister's Office, the individuals, or an official campaign statement.

Consult the debate organizer for the confirmed time, venue, attendance, accessibility, and media-accreditation details.

North Vancouver taxpayers deserve answers. The waste plant project has surged beyond its original $700 million estimate while critical red flags were raised—and the current mayor and council offered silence instead of oversight.

A project presented to the public with an already staggering price tag has continued to escalate, putting taxpayers at risk for even more.

When warning signs emerged, elected leaders should have demanded transparency, answers, and action—not stood by.

Graham is demanding a full forensic audit, clear answers from senior governments, and an end to treating taxpayers like a blank-check public ATM.

DNV residents deserve answers about corruption at City Hall and accountability from the Mayor and Council. Taking down transnational networks takes resolve. Watch Graham's story, then read the DNV Mayoral Corruption Accountability Report and the plan for transparent, accountable local government.

The winning campaign is built neighbourhood by neighbourhood

A stronger DNV starts with people who are ready to act. Choose one way to help today, then bring two neighbours with you.

Go beyond the campaign summary and follow Graham canvassing across the District of North Vancouver—listening to residents at a pivotal moment for DNV voters, safety, and civic freedoms.

The video also features Graham's business partner, Kyle Washington, Executive Chairman of Seaspan , sharing his perspective on the Mayor and District Council. Hear what he has to say, then decide for yourself.

I am Graham Alexander. A forensic audit of the wastewater plant. No injection sites forced into family neighbourhoods. Real fixes for gridlock. Off-grid shelters that solve homelessness without putting it on your street.

Support outreach, signs, literature, and a people-powered campaign.

Make your advance-voting plan and bring your neighbours with you.

I am Graham Alexander—and I am one of you: a person who wants safe communities, manageable roads, responsible spending, and a future our families can afford.

I bring the experience to do something about it: a UBC Electrical Engineering education, real estate development, complex infrastructure delivery, and the worldwide StayRunners technology business.

Through GGIQ Developments, Graham has worked on major development projects including Lynn Creek, Chilliwack Estates, Mount Thurston Drive, and Mount Archibald Place. The Mount Thurston and Mount Archibald hillside development in Chilliwack reflects the kind of vision, persistence, and delivery required to take a challenging site from concept to a finished community. Through StayRunners, he built and operated a worldwide technology business. He has led complex projects, systems, teams, and organizations from plan to delivery.

DNV needs a mayor who can read the plans, challenge the numbers, bring people together, and deliver. Graham's record in engineering, development, and business gives him the practical foundation to manage a municipality of 70,000 residents—not simply discuss its problems. This is a campaign for the highest standard of leadership: experienced, independent, accountable, and ready from day one.

That background is the reason Graham is prepared to deliver real change. Growth must strengthen DNV, not erase the neighbourhoods people chose to call home. Graham will focus new density around the Yaletown North transit hub, backed by private-capital investment in the roads, utilities, public spaces, and services it needs, while protecting the character of established communities including Seymour, Edgemont, Lynn Valley, and Grouse Woods.

This election is a choice about readiness. Voters deserve to compare every candidate’s experience, record, and ability to manage DNV’s complex projects and public money.

Graham brings electrical engineering training, major development delivery, global business leadership, and a record of taking on difficult accountability issues. Watch the comparison, then judge the qualifications for yourself.

A major international property dispute taught Graham what ordinary people face when systems fail to deliver clear answers, fair process, and accountability.

A Canadian businessman's fight to get his Mexican hotel back.

The Globe and Mail reported on the 2016 Tulum property dispute involving Graham and other hotel operators. The official ICSID case record also lists Graham as a claimant in the subsequent international arbitration.

A disputed eviction: The 2016 report says Graham's 24-room Tulum hotel was among properties affected during a contested beachfront land dispute.

A legal fight: It reports that Graham and other affected hotel operators pursued court injunctions and sought answers through legal and public channels.

Competing claims: The article describes disputed ownership claims and presents the differing positions of the hotel operators and people supporting the eviction.

This is an original summary of the linked Globe and Mail reporting, not a reproduction of the article.

Graham has firsthand experience navigating an international dispute involving property, legal process, and public institutions.

His experience reinforced a simple principle: people deserve transparent records, a fair hearing, and leaders who pursue the facts.

That is the standard Graham brings to municipal accountability: ask the questions, publish the facts, and keep working until residents get answers.

As Mayor, Graham will pursue an independent forensic review of the wastewater project, publish the contracts, change orders, costs, approvals, and timelines, and seek an appropriate independent investigation where the evidence warrants it.

If a review identifies avoidable losses, misconduct, or failures of oversight, Graham will seek every lawful avenue to recover public funds and pursue accountability. DNV taxpayers deserve the facts, a fair process, and a government that fights for their money.

This section summarizes independently available reporting and the official arbitration case record. It does not allege criminal wrongdoing by any individual or organization.

Graham Alexander's name recalls Alexander Graham Bell, the inventor and educator best known for his work on the telephone.

This historical reference is included as background about the candidate's name.

Straight from the doorstep: knocking on doors, hearing your concerns.

The best leadership starts with love for the place we share—and respect for the people who make it what it is.

I want a District where neighbours feel heard, families feel safe, small businesses can thrive, and every community—from Deep Cove to Lynn Valley, from the waterfront to the mountain—has a voice at the table.

That means listening first, working across differences, and staying close to the everyday realities behind the numbers. It means bringing people together around practical solutions, then doing the hard work to deliver them.

Graham Alexander is running for Mayor of the District of North Vancouver with a practical platform focused on preserving established neighbourhoods, accountable municipal spending, traffic relief, transit-oriented homes where growth belongs, and public services that work for residents.

You do not need another promise from a distant politician. You need somebody who understands the pressure of daily life in DNV and will take responsibility for solving it. I will put the facts on the table, stop waste, move DNV, protect children, and build smarter.

Order an immediate forensic audit of the reported $3.86B North Shore Wastewater Plant budget disaster. Publish the contracts, change orders, delays, approvals, and responsible decision points. Where evidence warrants it, refer matters to the RCMP and request international coordination through proper authorities.

The campaign is calling for lawful investigation; it does not claim that any person or organization has been found guilty.

I will not accept injection or supervised-consumption sites being forced into communities near daycares, schools, playgrounds, or child-centred spaces. Families should not be told that exposure to the risks of fentanyl and heroin is simply the price of living in their neighbourhood.

I will demand meaningful local consultation, safe siting, strong security, treatment pathways, and public accountability. Compassion and public safety must work together—and children must come first.

I will preserve the character of established neighbourhoods—including Edgemont, Lynn Valley, and Grouse Woods—by directing new density to Yaletown North around the transit hub. That growth must be matched by massive, upfront investment in roads, transit connections, utilities, public spaces, and community services so the area can flourish.

I will also fix bridge and arterial gridlock with modern traffic synchronization, federal USNA backing, and housing where people work. Support new rental construction connected to major employers such as Seaspan so workers can live closer to jobs instead of adding daily cross-North Shore congestion.

I will deploy AI-powered instant building permits to cut municipal review delays from months to minutes—while keeping accountable human oversight.

Residents deserve public timelines, responsible officials, project costs, safety standards, housing targets, and progress reports—not excuses. I will put every major commitment on the record and report back to the people.

I am Graham Alexander. I am like you: I want a safe community, responsible taxes, functional roads, and a government that listens. On October 17, vote for somebody who will do for the people.

Advance voting at District Hall, 355 W. Queens Rd. Confirm current hours before attending.

8 AM–8 PM. Check official sources for your assigned voting place and requirements.

The Plus Two Rule: every supporter can grow this movement. Bring two neighbours to our next canvass launch, or take two extra lawn signs for your block.

Career politicians see gridlock. Graham sees a plan: assemble the right land, negotiate the right deal, and deliver infrastructure that works for DNV taxpayers.

With experience in engineering, real estate development, hospitality, and global business, Graham brings the practical discipline to turn complex sites and stalled conversations into community-wide solutions.

Bring together multi-parcel opportunities and underused District land to create public value—not endless planning studies and missed opportunities.

Complex infrastructure takes serious negotiation with owners, agencies, and partners. Graham knows how to bring the right people to the table and move a project forward.

Intercept bridge traffic near Lynnmour, build strategic parking hubs, and connect reliable shuttles directly to Phibbs Exchange—while advancing housing and recovery solutions where they work.

Solving North Vancouver's homelessness crisis—with compassion.

Every mayor must lead with compassion for people experiencing homelessness. DNV can show the world what love, care, safety, and a real path forward look like.

Graham believes street-level crises require a better response: dignified support for people in need and safer public spaces for families, schools, daycares, and neighbourhoods. His campaign proposal is a dedicated, phased recovery facility away from residential centres, in the area behind Capilano University, subject to feasibility, public consultation, and required approvals.

Meet immediate needs with safe shelter, nutritious food, and stable care for people who need support before taking their next step.

Connect people with counselling, recovery supports, and practical care that rebuilds confidence and prepares them for independent living.

Create peaceful transitional housing with essential services and meaningful work opportunities so residents can earn, contribute, and move forward.

The goal is simple: compassionate support for people in need, and cleaner, safer neighbourhoods for every DNV family. That is love in action.

Your email is saved securely with the campaign mailing list. You can unsubscribe from any campaign email.

Watch Graham's campaign summary, then join the movement for real solutions in DNV.

I have watched a necessary public project — the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant — grow from a reported $700 million estimate in 2013 to $3.86 billion in 2024, and I have watched residents struggle to get a straight answer about how that happened or what it means for their tax bill. That is not a failure of engineering. It is a failure of reporting, oversight and accountability, and those are things a mayor can actually change.

In my working life, a project that tripled its budget would have triggered a review, a written explanation and a change in how the next one was run. Residents deserve the same standard from the government closest to them.

Faster municipal reviews and an assessment of District spaces for childcare.

I will propose a priority review stream for new and expanding childcare facilities, with early coordination between applicants, District staff and Vancouver Coastal Health.

I will seek an assessment of underused District-owned spaces that could host childcare, including conversion costs, accessibility and operating viability. Where feasible, operators will be chosen through a transparent process. Provincial capital funding will be pursued, but no space or grant will be counted until it is confirmed.

Success will be measured by licensed spaces that actually open.

Practical Leadership, Strong North Vancouver, United Canada Canada faces economic uncertainty, including tariff pressure and trade disputes with the United States. In difficult times, we must stand united as Canadians: supporting local businesses, protecting household budgets, and treating every tax dollar with care.

I have lived in North Vancouver for 38 years. I built my career here, raised my family here, and care deeply about this community. I am running for Mayor of the District of North Vancouver as an independent—with no slate and no party—because residents deserve a government that listens, explains how public money is spent, and takes responsibility when projects go off track. The North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant is one example. Metro Vancouver’s estimate rose from about $700 million in 2013 to $3.86 billion in 2024. The plant is necessary, but residents deserve public reporting, independent oversight, and a fair allocation of costs. I will advocate for all three wherever the District has a seat at the table.

My priorities are practical: predictable property taxes; housing for families, workers, and seniors that is supported by infrastructure while protecting neighbourhood character and green space; better coordination of road work and a united North Shore voice on transit; responsive municipal services; and stronger wildfire and emergency preparedness.

I bring an MBA in Global Management, a BSc in Computer Science, experience in business and operations, government and regulatory work, and service on three strata councils. Max Zahedi, max@maxformayor.ca

Ten priorities, each with the specific changes this campaign is committing to, how it is paid for, and what it means in your neighbourhood. Every promise here is written down so it can be checked.

I have lived in the District of North Vancouver for 38 years. I hold an MBA in Global Management and a BSc in Computer Science, and I have run a business, worked in software engineering and consulting, written policy for a Crown corporation and served on three strata councils. I will bring that experience with budgets, regulation and getting results to Municipal Hall.

At the first regular Council meeting , I will bring forward motions to launch the public commitment tracker and the North Shore wastewater fairness campaign.

I will bring forward practical proposals, build Council support and report openly on results. The Mayor is one vote of seven, so every commitment below says what I will propose, what Council must decide and what other governments control.

Every initiative that needs municipal resources will come with a proposed budget, funding source and schedule. Commitments involving other governments will name their responsibilities and the decisions still needed.

How this is paid for: new work will be funded only from savings that are verified and not already committed to existing services, and from confirmed partner contributions. Grants will not be counted until approved, and recurring programs will need recurring funding. Where money or staff are not available, projects will be phased, reduced or deferred, and I will say so publicly. These are targets and proposals, not a guaranteed delivery plan.

I will seek to work in partnership with the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úx̱wumixw (Squamish Nation) and səl̓ilw̓ətaʔł (Tsleil-Waututh Nation) on shared priorities, including emergency preparedness, the Maplewood and Deep Cove shorelines, and growth near Lions Gate and Norgate.

Proposal Deadlines count from the day the new council takes office. The mayor is one vote of seven, so each stop says what Max will propose, publish or ask for; what Council must decide is marked in each of the ten priorities.

Every promise tracked online within 100 days, updated quarterly, with a costed implementation plan within six months.

Fight for North Shore ratepayers on the $3.86 billion plant, including a fair share of the settlement money, an independent inquiry and senior-government funding.

3. Priority 3: Keep Property Taxes and Utility Bills in Check

A core service review and a target to keep municipal property-tax increases at or below B.C. inflation, with any increase above that explained publicly.

4. Priority 4: Pursue 1,000 Affordable Rental and Co-op Homes

A first-term target of 1,000 affordable rental and co-op homes secured with non-profit and co-op partners, counted only once sites, approvals and financing are committed.

5. Priority 5: Improve Traffic, Park Parking and Construction Coordination

A public top-ten list of District bottlenecks in 100 days, better construction coordination and simpler resident parking at parks.

6. Priority 6: Connect Development Decisions to Infrastructure Capacity

Clear public statements on pipes, roads, schools, transit and who pays before major rezonings and District growth plans. Pro-housing and pro-infrastructure.

7. Priority 7: Make the District Work for Local Business, Day and Night

One coordinating contact at Municipal Hall for businesses, service-time targets and a pilot for livelier evenings.

Faster municipal reviews and District spaces assessed for new childcare.

9. Priority 9: Strengthen School Safety and Address Drug Trafficking

A coordinated plan with the RCMP and School District to address drug activity near schools, and a public explanation of police staffing and when it returns to full strength.

10. Priority 10: Strengthen Wildfire and Disaster Preparedness

A risk-ranked preparedness plan, drills and support for residents who can’t simply drive away.

Each priority below lists what changes. These are campaign positions — where a number is quoted, its source is named at the foot of the page.

Within 100 days of taking office, I will publish a personal commitment tracker and seek Council support for an official municipal delivery dashboard.

The tracker will show original deadlines, Council decisions, outside dependencies, progress and evidence of completion. Proposed budgets and Council-approved budgets will be shown separately.

Updates will be published every quarter. Delays, revised targets and commitments that do not proceed will be explained openly.

Within six months of taking office, I will bring forward an initial implementation plan covering every priority and neighbourhood commitment. It will show existing District work that already meets part of each one, the extra staff time and spending needed, first-year actions versus later-term projects, and which items depend on funding or Council decisions.

The estimated program cost has grown from about $700 million to $3.86 billion. I believe North Shore ratepayers should not carry that increase alone.

Settlement money: Metro Vancouver received a $235 million settlement from the original contractor in May 2026. I will press for the largest possible share of those funds to benefit North Shore ratepayers, and for a public accounting of how the settlement is allocated.

Independent inquiry: I will support a full, independent inquiry into the cost overruns, and push for the fullest lawful public release of Metro Vancouver’s review and government responses.

Fair cost-sharing: I will seek Council’s appointment as the District’s representative on the Metro Vancouver board, and advocate for fairer regional cost-sharing. I will ask Victoria and Ottawa for capital funding, debt-servicing help and targeted ratepayer relief.

Resident petition: I will launch a North Shore wastewater fairness petition, open to residents, businesses and neighbouring councils.

Quarterly reports: I will report every quarter on advocacy, government responses and funding decisions, including what any relief means for a typical household bill.

Every dollar justified before Council asks residents for more.

In my first year, I will propose a core service review to find savings, duplication and services that could be delivered better.

I will seek Council support to set an annual budget target that holds the increase in the municipal property-tax levy on existing properties at or below inflation, measured by the previous year’s B.C. all-items Consumer Price Index. Any proposed increase above that benchmark will come with a public explanation of its causes, alternatives and effect on services. Utility fees, and costs set by Metro Vancouver, the Province or TransLink, will be shown separately.

Each budget will include a plain-language breakdown: what the District controls, what it does not, and what a typical homeowner and business will pay.

New spending in this platform will be funded from savings or partner contributions wherever possible. Grants will not be counted until approved, and any tax impact will be stated before Council votes.

A first-term target of securing sites, approvals and funding partnerships for 1,000 affordable rental and co-op homes.

I will work with non-profit, co-operative and other qualified housing partners on suitable District-owned and partner lands. The focus is rental and co-op housing, where affordability can be protected long-term.

What “secured” means: progress will be tracked at each stage: site identified, site secured, project approved, financing committed, under construction and occupied. A home will count toward the 1,000 target only once its site is secured, the project is approved and its financing is committed.

Affordability will be defined before any project is approved: income bands by household size, maximum rents (and whether utilities are included), and how long the affordability terms last, with a goal of at least 60 years.

Within my first year, I will bring forward a feasibility and financing plan naming available sites, realistic capacity, affordability levels and milestones. It will pursue provincial programs through BC Housing, including BC Builds for middle-income homes, and federal programs. Because BC Builds does not provide the ongoing subsidies lower-income households need, the plan will show separately how deeper affordability would be funded. No funding will be counted until committed.

If the evidence requires changes to the target, I will explain them publicly.

Where the law and funding agreements allow, I will support transparent local-connection criteria for residents facing displacement and people who work in our community, considered alongside income and housing need.

Read the full plan: who decides, what Max proposes, the trade-offs

A public list of District bottlenecks within 100 days, better coordination to reduce avoidable overlapping closures, and simpler resident parking at parks.

Within my first 100 days, I will seek Council support to publish an initial ranking of ten priority District traffic bottlenecks, using available delay, safety and traffic data, and flag where more study is needed before work can be designed.

I will bring forward a phased improvement plan with estimated costs, funding options and early actions.

I will propose a shared construction calendar that coordinates municipal, utility and development roadwork. Emergency work and projects controlled by others will be clearly marked.

On Highway 1, the bridges and the Ironworkers approach, which the Province controls, I will press the Province and TransLink for timelines and for coordination with District roadwork.

Park parking: I will propose simpler annual registration for the resident parking pass at parks including Deep Cove, Panorama and Whey-ah-Wichen / Cates, an option for people without smartphones, and fewer unnecessary repeat check-ins. A lot-by-lot review will balance turnover, accessible spaces and longer stays. Some changes may depend on the operator contract and technology, and any change will state its cost and effect on availability.

No major rezoning or District growth plan without a clear public answer on District infrastructure, who pays, and what depends on schools and transit.

I am not anti-housing. I am pro-infrastructure: new homes need the water, sewer, roads, schools and transit to support them.

I will propose public infrastructure-capacity and financing statements for major discretionary rezonings and District-led growth plans, consistent with provincial law. “Major” will be defined by Council using clear thresholds, such as the number of homes or floor area.

Each statement will show existing District capacity for water, sewer, drainage and roads, required upgrades, expected timing and who is expected to pay. It will separate confirmed funding from proposed contributions.

Schools, transit and other services controlled by partner agencies will be reported separately, as dependencies the District cannot guarantee.

The process will build on existing engineering work, with independent review where a project’s scale or risk warrants it.

One coordinating contact at Municipal Hall for your business, and a pilot for livelier evenings in our town centres.

I will propose a business concierge: one coordinating contact for commercial applications, expansions and small-business renovations.

I will ask for current processing times to be reported publicly, then propose realistic service targets based on that data, including a coordinated first response and a target time to decision for defined categories of complete applications. Reports will separate District review time from time waiting on applicants or outside agencies, and the proposal will include a staffing and cost assessment.

Processing times, missed targets and fixes will be reported publicly every quarter.

I will seek Council approval for a one-year evening activity pilot with businesses and community groups: food vendors, small live performances, community talent nights and voluntary extended hours. It will have a set budget, accessibility and operating conditions, and will be judged on attendance, neighbourhood impacts, safety and business results.

Investment outreach will focus on film, digital production and clean technology, while supporting the businesses already here.

Faster municipal reviews and an assessment of District spaces for childcare.

I will propose a priority review stream for new and expanding childcare facilities, with early coordination between applicants, District staff and Vancouver Coastal Health.

I will seek an assessment of underused District-owned spaces that could host childcare, including conversion costs, accessibility and operating viability. Where feasible, operators will be chosen through a transparent process. Provincial capital funding will be pursued, but no space or grant will be counted until it is confirmed.

Success will be measured by licensed spaces that actually open. Provincial licensing and safety rules remain in full effect.

Students deserve safe schools, safe routes home and protection from drug trafficking and exploitation.

I will seek a coordinated school-safety plan with North Vancouver RCMP, the North Vancouver School District and community partners to assess reported drug activity near schools and identify where more prevention and enforcement resources are needed.

I will advocate for visible patrols and focused enforcement where police evidence identifies trafficking or threats to students, while respecting the RCMP’s responsibility for operational decisions.

I will support clear reporting channels for students, parents and school staff, alongside drug education, early intervention and access to youth support services.

The District’s draft 2026–2030 financial plan shows RCMP staffing at 119 members, unchanged from 2025 and down from 129 in 2022, and anticipates a return to historical levels by 2030. I will request a public explanation of both the reduction and the restoration schedule, including whether it can be accelerated, separating authorized positions, funded positions, vacancies and officers available for duty.

Where the assessment identifies staffing gaps affecting public safety, I will bring forward a costed proposal with Council and the RCMP.

I will seek regular public progress reports that protect students’ privacy and ongoing investigations.

A risk-ranked plan with real targets, and a plan for residents who can’t simply drive away.

I will seek a risk-ranked prevention and preparedness work plan that first sets out current fuel-treatment and FireSmart property-assessment capacity, then sets measurable targets matched to available resources.

Working with North Shore Emergency Management, and seeking collaboration with neighbouring First Nations, I will support alert tests, tabletop exercises and voluntary community drills.

Plans will address people without vehicles, residents who need assistance and accessible emergency communication.

Preparedness will cover wildfire, smoke, extreme heat, flooding, earthquakes and power outages. Public guidance will make clear that real-time emergency instructions always come first.

The same ten priorities as one-line promises: the problem first, then what Max will do about it. Word for word what is on his VoteMate profile.

Know someone who should read this? Share the plan. Ten priorities, every commitment written down so it can be checked, and what each one means in your neighbourhood.

The ten priorities apply across the District. Here is what they mean in each area.

Parking: I will review check-in rules lot by lot and simplify resident access while keeping turnover, accessible spaces and longer-stay options.

Property standards: I will support consistent enforcement on neglected properties that meet legal thresholds, with fair notice and a right to reconsideration.

Drainage: Following the Gallant Avenue storm sewer work, I will ask for a public list of remaining drainage problems, ranked by risk, with engineering support and costs.

Chemtrade safety: I will seek a plain-language public summary of what the District can enforce, which agencies oversee other risks, and professionally prepared shelter-in-place and evacuation guidance.

Conservation areas: Where the District has lawful authority, I will seek to require that developments that could affect the foreshore or habitat come with the studies, safeguards and monitoring the responsible authorities can lawfully require, seeking collaboration with Tsleil-Waututh Nation.

Jobs: I will vote to keep the employment land that adopted plans set aside, and propose that any change show its effect on industrial activity and regional designations.

Maplewood: voting, meetings and more · Seymour: voting, meetings and more

Growth and infrastructure: I will ask for a public capacity check on pipes, roads, schools and transit, and, where the District has authority, phase discretionary growth with the upgrades it needs, while pressing the school district and TransLink on theirs.

Kilmer Road: I will publish what safety measures are in place, what is outstanding and what the speed, crossing and collision data show, and act on the results.

Eastview Park: I will act on documented noise, trail damage and parking problems through restoration, routing and enforcement while keeping the park open to the public.

Building size: I will ask for clear public information on what zoning allows on different lots, with modelling of privacy, shadowing, trees and housing effects.

Delbrook Avenue: I will publish the full history of safety changes and before-and-after results, and keep, fix or expand measures based on the evidence.

Wildfire readiness: I will support local exercises suited to this interface area, with plans for residents without vehicles or with mobility or communication needs.

Local business: Edgemont Village businesses will have access to the District-wide business concierge, with clear requirements and service targets.

Tourist traffic: I will seek agreement with attraction operators and TransLink to expand shuttles and transit where they would reduce car trips.

Trees: I will review how well tree bylaws actually protect healthy trees, including arborist review, construction protection, replacement and survival monitoring.

Phibbs Exchange: I will work with TransLink and the Province to address lighting, crossing and accessibility gaps, with a public list of who owns and funds each fix.

Industrial land: I will propose that rezoning applications show their effect on industrial capacity, business displacement and regional designations.

Childcare: I will include District-owned spaces here in the childcare space assessment.

Pemberton Heights traffic: If traffic evidence shows turning restrictions are warranted, I will support testing them as a monitored pilot that checks emergency access and whether traffic shifts to other streets.

Norgate flooding: I will ask for updated flood hazard information and a ranked list of drainage and coastal protections, with ownership, funding and maintenance spelled out, seeking collaboration with the Squamish Nation.

Lions Gate amenities: I will publish which public-space and transportation commitments are secured, what gaps remain and who is responsible for delivering them.

The District of North Vancouver describes itself as eight community areas. Each page below says where to vote, which all-candidates meeting is nearby, what the District lists for the area, and how Max Zahedi's priorities apply there.

One of the District's longest-established communities and one of its designated town centres.

Upper Lynn · Upper West Lynn · Lower West Lynn · Valley Centre · Central Lynn · Lynn Canyon · West Lynn Terrace · Boundary · Kirkstone

The District calls Lynn Creek one of its new town centres: bounded by Lynn Valley to the north, the waterfront industries to the south, the City of North Vancouver to the west and Highway 1 to the east, with new homes within walking distance of Phibbs Exchange, and home to Capilano University and to Seylynn, Bridgman and Inter River parks.

One of the four town centres designated in the Official Community Plan, close to the waterfront and to business and industry, with the Seymour River, the Burrard Inlet foreshore and mudflats, Maplewood Farm, Cutter Island Park and the Windridge Escarpment.

Riverside · Seymour Heights · Blueridge · McCartney Woods · Windridge · Windsor Park · Northlands · Parkway · Parkgate · Indian River · Roche Point

The northwest corner of the District, on the slopes below Grouse Mountain, bounded by Highway 1 to the south and Delbrook / Upper Lonsdale to the east, with its commercial and community heart in Edgemont Village, which the District is refreshing.

Grousewoods · Cleveland · Canyon Heights · Handsworth · Highlands · Edgemont · Edgemont Village

A primarily residential area between Upper Capilano, Lynn Valley and the City of North Vancouver, known for its views and park space.

Delbrook · Upper Delbrook · Norwood Queens · Carisbrooke · Braemar · Upper Lonsdale

The western gateway to the District and the first community after the Lions Gate Bridge, with the commercial area along Marine Drive.

Lower Capilano · Woodcroft · Pemberton Heights · Pemberton · Norgate

Confirmed fact The eight areas and the neighbourhoods inside them are the District of North Vancouver's own, from its "In your neighbourhood" pages, read September 12, 2026. Central Lonsdale, Lower Lonsdale, Grand Boulevard and Calverhall are in the City of North Vancouver, a separate municipality that elects its own mayor and council on the same day. If you live there, this election is not yours — the City's is.

Know someone who wants the election explained for their own street? Share this page. Eight community areas, each with where to vote, the all-candidates meeting and what Max proposes there.
