What this campaign does with your information, what this website is, and how to tell us when something on it does not work for you.

Only what you type into a form on this site. That may include your name, email address, telephone number, postal code, neighbourhood, address (for lawn sign requests), languages spoken, availability, the issues you care about and your message.

The site does not ask for, and must never be used to collect, financial account details, government identification numbers or passwords.

To meet record-keeping obligations under BC election law, where those apply.

Your information is used by the campaign team only. It is not sold, rented or traded . It is shared outside the campaign only where the law requires it — most relevantly, Elections BC requires campaigns to report contributions of $100 or more, including the contributor's name.

Campaign records are kept for as long as BC election law requires and are then deleted. If you ask to be removed from campaign communications before then, that request is honoured immediately.

Unsubscribe — every campaign email carries a working unsubscribe link, and you can also email the campaign directly.

Access — ask what the campaign holds about you and it will be provided.

Correction and deletion — ask for a correction or removal and it will be actioned, except where election law requires a record to be kept.

This site sets no advertising or tracking cookies, and carries no third-party analytics, advertising pixels or social media trackers. Opening a page contacts no company other than the one hosting it — the typefaces are served from this domain rather than from Google Fonts — with one exception: the map of voting places on the voting page, which is served by Google and loads as you scroll down to it. The Instagram posts at the top of the homepage are not an exception: this site’s own server fetches them from Instagram and serves their pictures itself, so your browser contacts Instagram only if you tap a post or the “Follow on Instagram” link. Your browser may store small preferences locally — a chosen language, whether you picked the light or dark theme, or an unsent form draft — which stays on your device and is never sent to the campaign. The only cookie this site ever sets is for the campaign’s own administrator while logged in; visitors get none.

The campaign counts visits to its own pages, on its own server, to see which pages people read and roughly where interest is coming from. Each page view sends one small message to this website containing the page, the site that linked to it (if any), your browser’s language setting, the width of your screen (to tell a phone from a desktop) and, on the voting page, which language you chose. No cookie is set and no outside service is involved. Your network address is used for two things and then discarded: to look up an approximate location — usually a city — in a database held on the campaign’s own server, and to make a scrambled daily identifier that lets the campaign count how many different people visited on a given day. That identifier changes every day and cannot be turned back into an address, so nobody can be followed from one day to the next, and the address itself is never stored. If your browser sends a Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control signal, nothing is sent at all. Counts are kept for no more than 13 months.

The campaign’s videos, the short one on the homepage, the eight-minute one and the short ones on the Farsi, Chinese and Tagalog pages, are served from this website, not from YouTube or any other company. If you play one, the same kind of message records that it was played, on which page, how many seconds of it you watched, the furthest point you reached and whether it reached the end, with the same scrambled daily identifier and the width of your screen. To keep those as one record, the page makes up a random code for that single page view; the code is not stored on your device and is gone when you leave the page. Nothing is recorded if you do not press play, or if your browser sends a Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control signal.

The voting page shows the District of North Vancouver’s map of voting places, which is served by Google Maps. It is not requested when the page opens; your browser loads it as you scroll down to the “Where to vote” section — at which point Google receives the request and may set its own cookies, as it would on any site carrying a Google map. The District’s own website, linked beneath the map, carries the same map.

The voting page, and the Chinese, Farsi and Tagalog pages, can show the voting places nearest you. It works on your own device: the page downloads one list of North Vancouver postal codes and their approximate positions from this website, and your browser compares your postal code with it. Your postal code is not sent to the campaign or to anyone else, and nothing is kept. If you press “Use my location”, your browser asks your permission first and then tells the page where you are; that stays on your device too, although your browser may use its own location service to work it out. The “Directions” links open Google Maps, which then receives the address of the voting place you chose, and nothing else from this site.

If you sign up for voting reminders or campaign updates, your name, email address, mobile number (if you gave one) and area are stored in a database on the campaign’s own server, outside the public web folder. No email-marketing company holds the list. The campaign records the date and time you agreed, the address the form was sent from, and the exact sentence you ticked, because Canada’s anti-spam law asks for that record. Emails are sent from this domain; every one carries a working unsubscribe link and the headers that let your mail program unsubscribe you in one click. Text messages are sent only to people who ticked the separate text-message box, through Twilio, a messaging carrier that receives your number and the message and nothing else; reply STOP to any text to end them. Unsubscribing closes that channel immediately. The record itself is kept for as long as BC election law requires and is then deleted.

The poll questions are anonymous. An answer is stored on the campaign’s own server with the question, the option chosen, the area you gave if you gave one, and the same scrambled daily identifier the visit counter uses, so that one person counts once per question per day. No name, email or address is stored with an answer, and nothing joins an answer to the contact list. Your browser remembers which questions you have answered so it can show you the results; “Change my answer” forgets that and your next answer replaces the earlier one for the day. Results for a question are shown to anyone who has answered it, with the number of answers, and the two questions marked “for the campaign only” are never shown to anyone outside the campaign.

If your connection drops while you are filling in a form, your answers are kept in your own browser so they are not lost. They stay on your device until you send them or clear your browser data.

This website is published by the campaign to elect Max Zahedi as Mayor of the District of North Vancouver.

Content is provided for information about the campaign. It is not legal, financial or professional advice.

Policy positions are commitments of intent by a candidate. A mayor is one vote on a council and cannot guarantee a council decision.

Election dates, voting places and voting rules are set by the District of North Vancouver and Elections BC. Where this site differs from them, they are correct .

Links to other websites are provided for convenience. The campaign does not control and is not responsible for their content.

Campaign text and images are the property of the campaign. Journalists and community groups may reproduce material from the media kit in coverage of the election.

Submitting abusive, fraudulent or automated content through the forms on this site is not permitted.

This site is built to meet WCAG 2.2 Level AA . Accessibility is not a feature of a campaign website; a voter who cannot read the voting information is a voter who was shut out.

Full keyboard navigation, with a visible focus indicator on every interactive element.

Colour contrast checked against AA thresholds for body text, headings and buttons.

Form fields with real labels, clear required-field marking, and error messages that name the problem.

Descriptive alternative text on images, and captions on published photographs.

Animation reduced automatically when your device asks for reduced motion.

A light and a dark theme, following your device by default and switchable from any page. Both were checked against the AA contrast thresholds, not just the light one.

Pages that remain readable and printable without JavaScript.

Translations of the voting essentials are pending review by native speakers.

The eight-minute video has English captions and Farsi subtitles, and the record page explains every graph in it in text.

The short videos on the Farsi, Chinese and Tagalog pages print every spoken sentence on screen, but have no separate transcript yet.

If any part of this site prevents you from getting the information you need, contact the campaign and it will be fixed. If you need campaign information in another format — large print, plain text, read aloud over the phone — ask and it will be provided.

Contributions to BC municipal campaigns are governed by the Local Elections Campaign Financing Act and administered by Elections BC.

Only individuals may contribute. Organizations, corporations, unions and associations may not.

Contributors must be residents of British Columbia and Canadian citizens or permanent residents .

Contributions of $100 or more are publicly reported, including the contributor's name.

You must contribute your own money . Being reimbursed by someone else, or contributing on another person's behalf, is prohibited.

Municipal campaign contributions do not receive tax receipts.

Contributions are accepted by Interac e-Transfer to donate@maxformayor.ca, into the campaign account controlled by the financial agent, who records the contributor's name and address. Card payments are not offered on this site.

This website is published by the campaign to elect Max Zahedi as Mayor of the District of North Vancouver. It is not a District of North Vancouver publication and it is not affiliated with the District, Metro Vancouver or Elections BC.

Voting dates, voting places and voting rules should always be confirmed through the District of North Vancouver and Elections BC.

Figures quoted about the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant are as reported by Metro Vancouver. Reported figures can change; readers are encouraged to check the source.

This statement is required on campaign advertising under BC election law and must be confirmed in its final wording by the campaign's financial agent before this site is published.

Know someone who wants to see how a campaign handles their data? Share this page. What the site collects, what it never does, and the rules on contributions, in plain words.

Thirty-eight years in North Vancouver. A business owner, an operations manager and a neighbour who believes a municipal government should be able to explain itself.

Max Zahedi is an independent candidate for Mayor of the District of North Vancouver, British Columbia, in the municipal election on Saturday, October 17, 2026. He has lived in North Vancouver for 38 years. He holds an MBA in Global Management and a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science. He has owned and operated businesses, managed operations, worked in government and regulatory settings, written policy and procedures for a Crown corporation, and served on three strata councils. He speaks English and Farsi. His campaign focuses on accountability for the cost of the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant, property taxes, housing, traffic, public safety and a more responsive municipal hall. He is not part of any party or slate.

On the ballot as Fardin Maximilian Zahedi . Max is the name he goes by.

This is where I built my life, raised my family and became part of a community I deeply care about. Through my work in technology, public service, business and community organizations, I have learned the value of listening, working with others and following through.

I am running for mayor because I know this community, understand the pressures residents are facing and believe I have the experience to improve how the District works for them.

I have watched a necessary public project — the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant — grow from a reported $700 million estimate in 2013 to $3.86 billion in 2024, and I have watched residents struggle to get a straight answer about how that happened or what it means for their tax bill. That is not a failure of engineering. It is a failure of reporting, oversight and accountability, and those are things a mayor can actually change.

In my working life, a project that tripled its budget would have triggered a review, a written explanation and a change in how the next one was run. Residents deserve the same standard from the government closest to them.

But this campaign is not only about one plant. It is about property taxes people can plan around, housing that matches what the infrastructure can carry, streets that are not permanently under construction, a district prepared for wildfire and earthquake, and a municipal hall that answers the phone.

My education is in both business and technology — an MBA in Global Management and a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science. That combination shapes how I approach public problems: understand the system, measure what it actually does, and report the result honestly even when it is not flattering.

Professionally I have worked in software engineering, owned and run businesses, managed operations, worked within government and regulatory environments, and consulted for other business owners. I have also spent years in community and cultural leadership across the North Shore.

My family lives here. My business life has been here. The trails, the creeks and the neighbourhood shops are not talking points to me — they are where I have spent the last four decades.

Publish the numbers, including the ones that are inconvenient.

Treat residents as the people who pay for this, because they are.

Know someone who has not met Max yet? Share this page. Who he is, why he is running and how he intends to work.

Family, neighbourhood and community photographs are added as the campaign takes them.

sources.text:
Experienced Leadership | Trusted Advocacy | Putting Students First

For more than 20 years, Cyndi Gerlach has been a dedicated leader in North Vancouver's public education community, serving students, families, and schools through volunteer leadership, PAC involvement, North Vancouver School District committees, and elected service. Her commitment to public education began long before she was elected, rooted in the belief that strong schools are built through collaboration, listening, and a shared commitment to ensuring every learner has the opportunity to succeed.

First elected as a School Trustee in the District of North Vancouver in 2011, Cyndi has proudly served four consecutive terms. During her time on the Board of Education, she has:

contributed to budget oversight, strategic planning, long-term facilities planning, policy development, and governance.

worked collaboratively with trustees, staff, educators, families, and community partners to address enrolment growth,

supported thoughtful long-term decisions that benefit students today and into the future

Cyndi has championed greater transparency in the School District's budget process, helping make financial decisions more accessible and understandable for families and the broader community while supporting responsible stewardship of public resources. She believes public trust is strengthened when communities understand how decisions are made and how resources are being used to support student success.

Cyndi has introduced more than 20 Board motions that have helped shape School District policy and governance. Her work has advanced initiatives supporting school environments related to:

Cyndi believes strong public education is built on responsible governance, meaningful community engagement, and decisions that always put students first. She is committed to listening respectfully, asking thoughtful questions, and making informed decisions that balance the needs of students today with the long-term sustainability of the School District. Guided by integrity, collaboration, and accountability , she believes every decision should maintain the trust and confidence of families and the broader community.

As an autistic leader and parent, Cyndi brings valuable lived experience to her role. Her perspective strengthens her commitment to removing barriers, improving accessibility, and ensuring students of all abilities and backgrounds are welcomed, valued, and supported. She believes each child deserves to feel they belong and that it is the responsibility of the education system to create environments where every learner can thrive.

Cyndi continues to contribute to education and governance at the provincial and national levels. She currently serves as Co-Chair of the Autism Alliance of Canada and has served on numerous boards, committees, and advisory groups focused on strengthening governance, advancing inclusive public policy, and improving outcomes for children, youth, and families. She brings those experiences back to North Vancouver, helping ensure the School District benefits from broader conversations, collaborative partnerships, and leading practices while keeping the needs of local students, families, and the community at the centre of her work.

My name is Rob Haines, and I am running for the School Trustee position in the next Municipal Election in the District of North Vancouver.

I've spent more than 23 years in public education because I've seen firsthand the difference a great teacher can make. That's what inspired me to become a teacher—the opportunity to make a meaningful difference in the lives of students, their families, and the communities that support them.​

🎓 Students First Every decision should focus on student success, well-being, and opportunity.

🏫 Strong Schools Supporting the educators, resources, and environments students need to thrive.

🌟 Bright Futures Creating pathways for every learner to reach their potential.

Throughout my career, I’ve taught in Ontario, Hong Kong, and British Columbia, giving me a broad perspective on different educational systems and approaches to student learning .

My experience includes roles as secondary classroom teacher, primary special education teacher, International Baccalaureate (IB) Diploma Programme educator, and Vice Principal. These experiences have allowed me to understand education from multiple perspectives—as a classroom teacher, a specialist supporting students with diverse learning needs, and a school leader working alongside students, families, educators, and support staff.

After more than two decades in education, I’m bringing this experience and perspective to my candidacy for North Vancouver School Trustee. I believe strong school leadership starts with listening, collaboration, and a clear focus on what matters most: student success.

As an educator, I believe every student deserves the opportunity to succeed. My experience in special education has shown me the importance of supporting students with diverse needs, while my work in advanced academic programs has reinforced the value of high educational standards and preparing students for future success.

Over my career, I’ve seen the challenges facing public education grow. Classrooms are becoming more complex, teachers and educational assistants are facing increasing demands, and staffing shortages are affecting both student learning and working conditions. I’m also concerned about literacy and numeracy outcomes and the pressures that inadequate funding can place on our schools.

I believe the answer is not to lower expectations, but to provide students with the support they need to meet them. I’m running for North Vancouver School Trustee to bring my experience in education and school leadership to the North Vancouver School Board and advocate for strong schools, meaningful support, and better outcomes for every student.

Rob Haines | School Trustee Candidate | District of North Vancouver 2026

I believe strong public schools require strong investment. As a North Vancouver School Trustee candidate, I’m committed to advocating for the resources students, educators, and families need to thrive.

That means advocating for greater investment in our North Vancouver schools, including funding to:

Address critical school infrastructure and facility upgrades

Above all, I remain committed to the principle that drew me to education more than two decades ago: helping young people thrive. I believe that when students, families, and educators are properly supported, our schools become stronger and our communities become healthier.

As a school trustee candidate for the District of North Vancouver 2026 School Board , I will bring my experience as an educator and school leader to advocate for students and help build strong schools and bright futures for North Vancouver.

background.quote: With over 20 years of global leadership experience in finance, strategy, and governance, the focus remains on translating public resources into measurable, real-world impact inside every classroom.

This inspired me to develop a children’s book designed to help young readers build cultural confidence. I am also working on a second book project focused on financial literacy, introducing basic concepts of money in a developmentally appropriate way and helping children develop essential life skills and healthy financial habits that support long-term success.

​Leaving a successful financial career wasn’t a loss; it was a deliberate choice. I transitioned into leadership development and equity-focused work because I believe real growth happens when systems are designed with people at the center.

That experience became the catalyst for my community work. I began creating and leading programs focused on cultural confidence, integration, and financial literacy first for adults, then for children. I wanted to start early, to give children the tools I wish more of us had growing up: confidence in who they are, comfort with money, and a sense of agency in the world. Teaching financial literacy from the preschool years onward became one of the most meaningful parts of my work.

As a board member, community advocate, and early-childhood financial literacy leader, I support financial inclusion, equitable practices, and inclusive growth that benefits communities and economies alike.

As a mother of two children in our public schools, I care deeply about the education our students experience today and the world we are preparing them for tomorrow.​Lynn Valley and North Vancouver are our home. Over the past decade, I have grown deep roots here volunteering in our schools, serving on non-profit boards, and bringing financial literacy directly into elementary classrooms.
Another outcome of this transition took shape while living in Canada, a country with open borders and a welcoming, multicultural environment that aligns closely with my equity initiatives.

As an Independent Business Advisory Consultant | Oxford & Yale Alum | Yale World Fellow: I work across North America and the Middle East, partnering with youth, startups, businesses, and communities to strengthen strategy, governance, financial literacy, and equity-driven impact.
My education at Oxford and Yale, and my experience as a Yale World Fellow, sharpened my global perspective but it was lived experience that truly shifted my path.

Every child deserves an education that equips them with the confidence, resilience, and practical life skills to thrive: empowering them not simply to navigate the world around them, but to shape it.

As a mother, volunteer, and community member, I believe we have a responsibility to leave our community better than we found it. I believe in building a community where our children feel a sense of belonging, learn to care for one another, and understand that they are not simply here to benefit from the world we inherit, but to help shape it and ultimately, to leave it even better for the generation that comes after them.

I’ve learned that community isn’t built by simply talking about what could be better. It’s built in the everyday moments by showing up, volunteering at school, supporting a child, listening to a parent, bringing people together, and finding ways to make things better. ​

As an Independent Business Advisory Consultant | Oxford & Yale Alum | Yale World Fellow: I work across North America and the Middle East, partnering with youth, startups, businesses, and communities to strengthen strategy, governance, financial literacy, and equity-driven impact.

As a board member, community advocate, and early-childhood financial literacy leader, I support financial inclusion, equitable practices, and inclusive growth that benefits communities and economies alike.
sources.title: Raheela Khan

sources.text:
Thank you for being here. Every career has a "why." Mine began in the financial markets, working at the intersection of economics, investment strategy, and public influence. From managing institutional portfolios to collaborating with regulators, shaping PR and media strategies, and sharing financial insights on television. I spent years in fast-paced, high-impact work shifting systems at an economic level.

Over time, I recognized a recurring barrier: self-exclusion. I saw how cultural confidence and self-doubt often caused people to opt out of pathways before they even began.

Today, my work centers on youth, communities, and systems. I focus on building cultural confidence and life skills, creating pathways that ensure everyone has the tools to participate fully. ​

My story is one of transition from finance to purpose, from metrics to meaning. It’s about building bridges across cultures, generations, and systems, and using knowledge, access, and experience to open doors for others. ​ For a long time, my world revolved around numbers, managing financial portfolios, markets, performance. I built a successful career in global finance, managing large-scale investments across regions and economies. On paper, it all made sense. Yet, somewhere along the way, I began to notice what the numbers didn’t show: the people left out of the system, the untapped potential, and the quiet cost of exclusion.

Working across both emerging economies and established western systems gave me a front-row seat to how access (or the lack of it) shapes lives. I saw how financial systems could either empower communities or unintentionally widen social gaps.

My education at Oxford and Yale, and my experience as a Yale World Fellow, sharpened my global perspective but it was lived experience that truly shifted my path. Becoming a mother changed the way I understood leadership, resilience, and responsibility. It made equity personal. It made inclusion urgent.

I experienced, firsthand, how easy it is for people especially women, immigrants, and newcomers to shrink themselves, to self-exclude, or to feel they don’t quite belong. That experience became the catalyst for my community work. I began creating and leading programs focused on cultural confidence, integration, and financial literacy first for adults, then for children. I wanted to start early, to give children the tools I wish more of us had growing up: confidence in who they are, comfort with money, and a sense of agency in the world. Teaching financial literacy from the preschool years onward became one of the most meaningful parts of my work.

Another outcome of this transition took shape while living in Canada, a country with open borders and a welcoming, multicultural environment that aligns closely with my equity initiatives. This inspired me to develop a children’s book designed to help young readers build cultural confidence. I am also working on a second book project focused on financial literacy, introducing basic concepts of money in a developmentally appropriate way and helping children develop essential life skills and healthy financial habits that support long-term success.

​Leaving a successful financial career wasn’t a loss; it was a deliberate choice. I transitioned into leadership development and equity-focused work because I believe real growth happens when systems are designed with people at the center. Today, my work focuses on advancing diversity, equity, and inclusion, empowering women and youth, and supporting responsible funding that creates both impact and sustainability.

Let’s Connect Whether you're interested in consulting, collaboration, speaking engagements, or community initiatives, I’d love to hear from you. Email: raheelakhan.com@gmail.com

Innovation & Technology : Technology and innovation can enhance teaching and learning when used thoughtfully and responsibly. I support approaches that help students develop the skills, knowledge, and digital competencies needed for success in a changing world.

Fiscal Responsibility : Public education depends on responsible stewardship of public resources. I am committed to transparent decision-making, sound financial management, and ensuring resources are directed toward supporting student learning and success.

Sustainability : Schools have an important role to play in building a more sustainable future. I support environmentally responsible practices that reduce our environmental footprint and help students become informed and engaged global citizens.

Good Governance : Strong governance helps build trust and supports effective decision-making. I am committed to collaboration, accountability, transparency, and respectful engagement with students, families, staff, and the broader community.

Strong public education is built on partnerships. I will continue to listen to diverse perspectives, bring people together, and work collaboratively with students, families, educators, staff, and community partners to ensure North Vancouver remains a place where every student can learn, grow, and reach their full potential.
